**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verses 1–5:**

(Makkan [except verse 38, and from verse 83 to verse 101, which are Madinan], with 110 verses [revealed after Surat al-Ghashiyah]) In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

God taught His servants and gave them understanding of how to praise Him and extol Him for His most abundant blessing upon them, which is the blessing of Islam, and for what He sent down upon His servant Muhammad (ﷺ) of the Book, which is the means of their salvation and success. ﴿And has not made in it any crookedness﴾: He has never made any crookedness in it at all. Crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in physical things. The intended meaning is the negation of contradiction and inconsistency from its meanings, and the negation of anything in it departing from wisdom and correctness.

If you ask: With what is ﴿upright (qayyiman)﴾ in the accusative? I say: It is better that it be governed by a hidden verb, and not be made a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the Book," because His saying ﴿and has not made﴾ is conjoined to "sent down," so it falls within the scope of the relative clause (silah). Whoever makes it a circumstantial qualifier of "the Book" separates the circumstantial qualifier from its referent by part of the relative clause. Its implied sense is: "and has not made for it a crookedness; rather He made it upright," because when He negated crookedness from it, He affirmed for it straightness.

If you ask: What is the benefit of combining the negation of crookedness with the affirmation of straightness, when either one would suffice without the other? I say: its benefit is emphasis (ta'kid), for a straight thing may be testified to as straight and yet it is not free of slight crookedness when one travels along it and examines it closely.

It has also been said: ﴿upright﴾ over all other books, confirming them and bearing witness to their truth. And it has been said: ﴿upright﴾ in regard to the welfare of the servants and the legislation they cannot do without. And it has been read as qayyiman.

"Warn" (andhara) is transitive to two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [78:40].

So one of the two objects was omitted. Its original form is ﴿to warn those who disbelieve of a severe might (ba's shadid)﴾. The word ba's (might/severity) derives from His saying ﴿with a painful punishment (bi-'adhabin ba'ees)﴾, and it is said: the punishment became severe (bu'isa al-'adhab), and the man became severe (ba'isa ba'san and ba'aasatan).

﴿from Him (min ladunhu)﴾: issuing from His presence. It has been read as min ladunhu with the dal pronounced with sukun, with the damma indicated (ishmam) and the nun with kasra.

﴿and give good tidings (wa-yubashshira)﴾: it is read both with the lightened and the intensified form.

If you ask: Why was it limited to one of the two objects of "warn"? I say: The object of warning has been made the principal aim that is anticipated, so it was necessary to limit it to that one.

The evidence for this is the repetition of the warning in His saying ﴿and warn those who say, "God has taken a son"﴾, which is linked to "the warners" without mentioning what they are warned about, just as the object of the good tidings was mentioned in His saying ﴿that for them is a good reward﴾, being dispensed with because it was mentioned earlier.

The good reward is Paradise.

﴿They have no knowledge of it (ma lahum bihi min 'ilm)﴾, i.e., of the son or of taking him, meaning that this saying of theirs did not come from knowledge, but from extreme ignorance and imitation of their fathers. Their fathers were seized (ishtamalathu) by Satan and his enticement. [[His saying "wa-qad ishtamalathu" perhaps is: istamalathu, with unpointed sin and sukun on the mim. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: The taking of a son by God is impossible in itself, so how is it said ﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾? I say: The meaning is "they have no knowledge of it," because it is not something that can be known, owing to its impossibility. The absence of knowledge of a thing is either due to ignorance of the path leading to it, or because it is itself impossible, so that knowledge of it cannot properly be related to it. [[Mahmud said: "If you say the taking of a son by God is impossible in itself, how is it said to them ... etc." Ahmad said: It has previously been mentioned in His saying ﴿and that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ [3:151] that this comes in the form of mockery (tahakkum); otherwise there is no authority for polytheism to be sent down. Its parallel is the line:

"and the lizard does not burrow therein"

And I had previously stated that the speech comes in the sense of reality and the basic meaning, and that the negation of sending down authority sometimes is because its sending down and existence is impossible, and sometimes because it has not occurred even though it is possible. And God knows best.]]

It was read: ﴿kabura kalimatan (how great a word)﴾ and ﴿kalimatun﴾, with the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) and with the nominative as subject (fa'il). The accusative is stronger and more emphatic. It carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How great a word it is!"

﴿that comes out of their mouths (takhruju min afwahihim)﴾ is a qualifier of "word," expressing the magnitude of their audacity in uttering it and letting it out of their mouths. For many things that Satan whispers into people's hearts and that they speak of to themselves, which are abominations, they cannot restrain themselves from blurting them out and letting their tongues utter them. Rather, they suppress them out of aversion (tashawwur) from making them manifest, as one recoils from exposing one's nakedness. How then should one act with such an abomination? [[His saying "tashawwuran min izharih" means: distancing from its manifestation, as if it were a nakedness. In the Sihah, "al-shawar" is the pudendum. From it comes the saying: "shawwara bihi," as if he uncovered his nakedness. (ʿ)]]

It was also read: kabura with the ba' sukun and the damma indicated (ishmam).

If you ask: To what does the pronoun in "kabura" refer? I say: To their saying ﴿God has taken a son﴾, and it is called a "word" just as poems are called by that name.

[[Mahmud said: "If you say the taking of a son by God is impossible in itself, how is it said to them ... etc." Ahmad said: It has previously been mentioned in His saying ﴿and that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾ [3:151] that this comes in the form of mockery (tahakkum); otherwise there is no authority for polytheism to be sent down. Its parallel is the line:

"and the lizard does not burrow therein"

And I had previously stated that the speech comes in the sense of reality and the basic meaning, and that the negation of sending down authority sometimes is because its sending down and existence is impossible, and sometimes because it has not occurred even though it is possible. And God knows best.]]

It was read: ﴿kabura kalimatan (how great a word)﴾ and ﴿kalimatun﴾, with the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) and with the nominative as subject (fa'il). The accusative is stronger and more emphatic. It carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How great a word it is!"

﴿that comes out of their mouths (takhruju min afwahihim)﴾ is a qualifier of "word," expressing the magnitude of their audacity in uttering it and letting it out of their mouths. For many things that Satan whispers into people's hearts and that they speak of to themselves, which are abominations, they cannot restrain themselves from blurting them out and letting their tongues utter them. Rather, they suppress them out of aversion (tashawwur) from making them manifest, as one recoils from exposing one's nakedness. How then should one act with such an abomination? [[His saying "tashawwuran min izharih" means: distancing from its manifestation, as if it were a nakedness. In the Sihah, "al-shawar" is the pudendum. From it comes the saying: "shawwara bihi," as if he uncovered his nakedness. (ʿ)]]

It was also read: kabura with the ba' sukun and the damma indicated (ishmam).

If you ask: To what does the pronoun in "kabura" refer? I say: To their saying ﴿God has taken a son﴾, and it is called a "word" just as poems are called by that name.

The Prophet's state is compared with that of a man whose beloved ones and dear kin have left him: they turned away from him and did not believe in him, and he was overcome by grief and sorrow over their turning away. He is like one who sheds tears of regret over their traces and destroys himself in grief and longing for their separation. It is read "bākhiʿun nafsaka" (destroying yourself), in the original form, and with the genitive construction (iḍāfah), meaning: its killer and destroyer. It refers to the future for the one who reads "in lam yu'minū" (if they do not believe), and to the past for the one who reads "an lam yu'minū," meaning: because they did not believe in this discourse, i.e., the Qur'an, "asafan" is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: due to excessive sorrow. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

As for al-asaf (ʾasaf, grief/anger), it means extreme intensity of sorrow and anger. It is said: "rajul asif" and "asīf" (a man who is grieved or angered).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 7–11:

﴿مَا عَلَى الْأَرْضِ﴾ means: what is fit to be an adornment for it and for its people, of the ornaments of this world and what is considered beautiful in it. ﴿لِنَبْلُوَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا﴾. The good deed (husn al-'amal) is: abstention from it (zuhd) and not being deceived by it. Then He made abstention from inclining towards it by His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّا لَجاعِلُونَ مَا عَلَيْها﴾, meaning this adornment, ﴿صَعِيداً جُرُزاً﴾, meaning like a white land with no vegetation in it, after it had been green and grassy, in the removal of its brightness, the effacing of its beauty, and the nullifying of what made it an adornment: the causing of animals to die and the drying up of plants and trees, and the like. He mentioned, among the universal signs, the adorning of the earth with what He created ﴿فَوقها﴾ [[His saying "mimma khalaqa" (from what He created) is perhaps "bima khalaqa" (with what He created). (ʿ)]] of kinds that cannot be counted, and the removal of all that, as if it had never been. Then He said: ﴿أَمْ حَسِبْتَ﴾, meaning: that is greater than the story of the People of the Cave and the preservation of their lives for a long period. Al-Kahf: the wide cave in the mountain. ﴿وَالرَّقِيمِ﴾ is a name for all of them. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"And there is nothing there but al-Raqim, neighbouring [its] threshold, and their hunting dog, while the people are sleeping in the cave."

[[By Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. Al-Raqim: the dog of the People of the Cave. Al-Wasid: the courtyard of the house, its door and threshold, and the house may contain it. Al-Hamd: plural of hamid, i.e. sleeping. Al-Qawm: conjoined to al-Raqim. He says: there is nothing in that desert except the dog, in the state of being adjacent to the courtyard of their cave, and except the people, in the state of their being asleep in the cave, i.e. the cave.]]

It is said: it is a lead tablet on which their names were inscribed, placed at the door of the cave. It is said: the people had recorded their story by carving it into the mountain. It is said: it is the valley in which the cave is. It is said: the mountain. It is said: their town. It is said: their place between Ghadban and Ayla, short of Palestine. ﴿كانُوا آيَةً عَجَباً مِنْ آياتِنا﴾: described by the verbal noun, or in the sense of "a wondrous sign". ﴿مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً﴾, i.e. mercy from the treasuries of Your mercy, which is forgiveness, provision, and security from enemies. ﴿وَهَيِّئْ لَنا مِنْ أَمْرِنا الذي نحن عليه﴾ from separation from the disbelievers ﴿رَشَداً﴾, so that through it we may be rightly guided and rightly guiding; or: make our affair entirely rightness, like your saying: "I saw from you a lion." ﴿فَضَرَبْنا عَلَى آذانِهِمْ﴾, i.e. We struck over their ears a veil from hearing, meaning: We put them to sleep with a heavy sleep in which sounds do not rouse them, as you see one deeply asleep being shouted at and not hearing or waking. The object, which is the veil, is omitted, as one says: "He built upon his wife," meaning: he built the dome over her. ﴿سِنِينَ عَدَداً﴾: countable years. It may mean either abundance or fewness, since a large number is small in His sight, like His saying: ﴿لَمْ يَلْبَثُوا إِلَّا ساعَةً مِنْ نَهارٍ﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: when the number is small, its quantity is understood and there is no need to count it; when it is large, it needs to be counted.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 12:

"Ayyu" (which of) contains the meaning of interrogation, so it suspends the verb "li-na'lama" (that We might know) from acting upon it, and it is not governed by it. It has also been read "liya'lama" (that He might know), which is likewise suspended, because its nominative status comes from the inceptive (mubtada') and not from the attribution of "ya'lamu" to it; the subject of "ya'lamu" is the content of the clause, just as it is the object of "na'lama". ﴿Which of the two parties was more accurate in computing the time they had stayed﴾, because when they awoke they disagreed about that. This is His saying: ﴿One of them said, "How long have you stayed?" They said, "We have stayed a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have stayed."﴾ Those who said "Your Lord knows best how long you have stayed" were those who recognised that their stay had been prolonged. Or "ayyu al-hizbayn al-mukhtalifayn" (which of the two disagreeing parties) refers to others besides them. "Ahsa" is a past-tense verb, meaning: which of them kept count of ﴿the time they had stayed﴾.

[[Mahmud said: "Ahsa is a past-tense verb, meaning: that We might know which of them kept count of the time ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Some grammarians made the pattern "af'ala" from a derived form containing a hamza a regular analogy, and claimed this to be the position of Sibawayh, giving as its reason that its formation from it does not alter the structure of the word, but is merely the substitution of one hamza for another.]]

Ahsa is a past-tense verb, meaning: which of them kept count of ﴿the time they had stayed﴾.

Ahmad said: [the second part of this note is preserved in the translation above].

Now, if you say: what do you say about the one who made it an elative (af'al al-tafdil)? I answer: this is not the sound view, because its formation from a non-triliteral bare root is not analogical, and examples such as "a'da min al-jarab" (more hostile than mange) and "aflas min Ibn al-Mudhallaq" (more destitute than Ibn al-Mudhallaq) are anomalous. Analogy based on an anomaly outside the Qur'an is impermissible, so how much more so within it? Moreover, "amadan" (a period) must either be governed by the elative "af'al", which it cannot be since the elative does not govern, or be governed by "labithu" (they stayed), but then the meaning would not hold together. If you claim that I govern it by a supplied verb indicated by "ahsa", as was supplied in the line:

"And strike with the sword the crowns [of the enemy's heads]..."

[[Poetry: "I have not seen a tribe, a dawn-visited tribe, like ours; nor, on the day we met, horsemen like ours. More staunch and more protective of what is sacred than they are, and striking harder with swords at the helmets. When we press a charge against them, they face us with the thoroughbred horses and the wavering spears. When horses turn away from a fallen comrade we have dragged back, they return only with scowling faces." It is attributed to al-Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami; "al-hayy" means the Banu Zubayd of Yemen. "Akarr" means more fierce in charging; "ahmaa" means more protective; "al-haqiqa" is what is worth defending of honour and property. "Al-qawanis" is the plural of "qunus", the top of a warrior's helmet and the top of a horse's head. "Al-madhakki" are noble horses which have passed a year after their wounds; "al-mada'is" are the unyielding spears with which one thrusts. "Al-da's" is a trace, and "al-mada'asa" is the thrusting. "Ya'bis" is ... etc. In one narration "jalat" replaces "halat", meaning: turned toward a side; "al-hawl" with a ha' is a change of direction. "Al-sari'" is one thrown down on the ground; "nakruha" means we bring them back; "al-awabis" are those with faces darkened by the dust of the charge. "Hayyan musbihan" means one who comes in the morning. "Mithl al-hayy" is an accusative of state if "ra'a" is visual, or a second object if it is cognitive; "Akarr" is a substitute for "hayyan". It cannot be taken as an adjective or second object, because if you said "I have not seen the like of Zayd a man more excellent than him", the meaning would only be sound as an apposition, since likeness contradicts preference, unless likeness is in one attribute and preference in another, in which case there is no obstacle. "Adrib" is an elative, a substitute for "fawaris" as previously explained, and so it is a chiasmic (laff wa nashr) arrangement in order. The elative does not govern an object in the accusative; indeed consensus has been reported on this. Thus "al-qawanis" is accusative by an omitted verb, meaning "they strike the crowns, i.e. the heads". But Muhammad ibn Mas'ud said in his book al-Badi': "Whoever says the elative does not govern a direct object is mistaken," and he cited this line and others. He praised both sides in saying: "When we press a charge against them once, they meet us with thoroughbred horses and good spears, so they are brave. And in saying: when our horses turn or swerve from a slain comrade of ours, we bring them back against the enemy for vengeance, and they return only with scowling faces; so we are braver than they."]]

Strike the crowns: you have pushed away the nearby meaning when you refused to take "ahsa" as a verb, and then were compelled to return to supplying and implying it. If you ask: how did God make knowing their counting of the period a purpose of striking upon their ears? I answer: God, glorified is He, has always known this; rather, He intended what the knowledge involved of the matter becoming manifest to them, so that they might increase in faith and reflection, and that it might be a kindness to the believers of their time and a clear sign for the unbelievers.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 13–15:

"And We increased them in guidance" (وَزِدْناهُمْ هُدىً) through success (al-tawfiq) and steadfastness (al-tathbit). "And We fortified their hearts" (وَرَبَطْنا عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ), and strengthened them through patience (al-sabr) in abandoning homelands and comfort, and in fleeing with their religion to some of the caves (al-ghayran), and We emboldened them to stand by the word of truth and to openly display Islam, "when they stood up before the tyrant" (إِذْ قامُوا بين يدي الجبار), who was Daqyanus, without any concern for him when he rebuked them for abandoning the worship of the idol. "So they said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth..." (فَقالُوا رَبُّنا رَبُّ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ) ... "shatatan" (شَطَطاً): a statement that is shatat, which is excessive wrongdoing and going far in it, from shatta: when it is far. From it comes ashatta in bargaining and in other matters. "Hā'ulā'" (هؤُلاءِ) is a subject (mubtada'), "qawmunā" (قَوْمُنَا) is an explanatory appositive ('atf bayan), and "ittakhadhū" (اتَّخَذُوا) is the predicate (khabar). It is a statement that carries the meaning of denial (inkar). "Lawla ya'tūna 'alayhim" (لَوْلا يَأْتُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ): why do they not bring upon them (proof), i.e., "why do they not bring proof for their worship," so the modified noun has been omitted. "Bi-sultanin bayyin" (بِسُلْطانٍ بَيِّنٍ): clear authority. This is a rebuke, because bringing authority for the worship of idols is impossible. It is evidence for the invalidity of blind imitation (al-taqlid), and that religion necessarily requires proof in order for it to be sound and established. "Iftara 'ala Allahi kadhiban" (افْتَرى عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِباً): by attributing a partner to Him.

And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah, [this is] an address from some of them to others, at the time their resolve to flee with their religion had been firmed up. "And what they worship" is in the accusative, coordinated with the pronoun [in "them"]; meaning: when you withdrew from them and from what they worshipped. "Except Allah" may be a continuous exception (istithna' muttasil), according to what is narrated: that they used to acknowledge the Creator while associating others with Him, as the people of Makkah did. And it may be a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati'). It has also been said that it is an interjected statement (kalam mu'taridh), an announcement from Allah Most High about the youth (al-fityah) that they did not worship other than Allah.

"A support" (mirfaqan): it is read with a fatha and with a kasra on the mim, and it means what one derives benefit from, i.e., what one profits by. [Allah says this] either because they say that out of confidence in the grace of Allah and strength in their hope, due to their reliance on Him and the clarity of their certainty; or because a prophet of their era informed them of it; or because some of them were prophets.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 17:

تَتَزاوَرُ (tatazawaru): meaning tamayyalu (inclines). Its origin is tatazawwaru, which is lightened either by assimilating the tā' into the zāy or by deleting it. Both have been read. It has also been read tazawwaru, and tazawwārru, on the pattern of tahammara and tahammāra. All of these derive from al-zawr, which is inclination, and from it comes zārahu, when he inclined towards him. Al-zawr is inclination away from truth. "Dhāt al-yamīn" means the direction of the right side, and this is its literal sense. Taqriduhum (تَقْرِضُهُمْ) means taqta'uhum (cuts them off), not "brings them near"; it carries the sense of severance and cutting off. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Toward caravans that cut across the sides of the highland's ridges, leaving to the left and the right of them the horsemen [of the tribe]."

[[I looked upon the Jur'a al-Sibkha with a glance at morning, and the black of the eye in the water was restless.

Toward caravans that cut across the sides of the highland's ridges, leaving to the left and the right of them the horsemen [of the tribe].

By Dhu al-Rummah. Jur'a al-Sibkha is the name of a place, and the preposition-plus-noun phrase is attached to an implied circumstantial element (ḥāl) of the subject. "Ḍuḥā" is an adverbial of time, and "wa-sawād al-ʿayn..." (the black of the eye...) is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya). "Fī al-māʾ" (in the water) means: the tears are shāmis, that is, very agitated and turbulent. It is said: shamasa al-faras wa al-rajul shumūsan, when his temperament became bad. The ẓaʿīna is the woman in the howdah, or the mount upon which a woman sits, or the howdah in which there is a woman; the plural is ẓaʿn, ẓaʿn, aẓʿān, and ẓaʿānī. Yaqriḍna means yaqṭaʿna (they cut across). Aqwāz Mushrif are the upper parts of a mountain called Mushrif. It is also narrated as ajwāz, plural of jawz, meaning passage and road, that is: they separate him from them. Shimālan means the direction of the north. Al-Fawāris is the name of a place; treating it as the plural of fāris (horseman) is also possible, as it has been said, though the parallelism (muqābala) rejects it.]]

وَهُمْ فِي فَجْوَةٍ مِنْهُ (wa-hum fī fajwatin minhu): they are in a spacious area of the cave. The meaning is that they are in shade throughout their day, the sun not striking them at its rising or its setting, although they are in a wide, open place exposed to the sun, were it not that God screens it from them. It has been said: in a spacious part of their cave where they receive the breath of air and the coolness of the breeze, and they do not feel the oppression of the cave. ذلِكَ مِنْ آياتِ اللَّهِ (dhālika min āyāti llāh): what God did for them, namely the sun's deviation from them and its inclining away at rising and setting, is one of His signs, meaning that whatever lies in that direction would be struck by the sun while it does not strike them, as a special honor for them. It has been said: the cave's entrance faces north, toward the Banāt Naʿsh, so they are always in a place not reached by the sun (maqnaʾa) [[His saying "fa-hum fī maqnaʾa" (so they are in a shaded place): in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, Abu ʿAmr said: "al-maqnaʾa" and "al-maqnūʾa" are the places the sun never reaches. He also said: "ghayr maqnāt" and "maqnūw" without hamza, the opposite of al-maḍḥāt. (ʿ)]] always. The meaning of "that is among the signs of God" is that their condition and their story are among the signs of God.

مَنْ يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَهُوَ الْمُهْتَدِ (man yahdi llāhu fa-huwa l-muhtad): this is praise of them, for they strove for God and submitted their faces to Him, so He showed them kindness, helped them, and guided them to attain that noble honor and that special great sign. Every one who follows the path of the rightly guided is the one who attains success and is led to happiness, while whoever exposes himself to abandonment will find no one to protect and guide him after God's abandonment.

And you would think them awake, [while] they are asleep, with the sin of ﴿you would think them﴾ vocalized with a kasra and with a fatha: it is addressed to everyone. *Al-ayqaz* is the plural of *yaqz* (awake), like *ankad* in *nakad* (a plural pattern for an adjective of this form). It was said: their eyes were open while they slept, so the observer would think them awake. It was also said: because of how much they turned over. And it was said: they turned over twice a year. It was also said: they turned over once, on the day of ʿAshura'.

It was recited as *wa-yuqallibuhum* with the ya', the pronoun referring to God Most High. It was also recited as *wa-taqlibuhum*, as a verbal noun in the accusative, its accusative governed by a implied verb indicated by ﴿and you would think them awake﴾, as if it were said: "and you see and witness their turning."

Jaʿfar al-Sadiq recited *wa-kalbuhum*, meaning "and their dog's owner," ﴿spreading out his two forearms﴾, a narration of a past state. This is because the active participle does not govern when it has the sense of the past. Its genitive construction, when made genitive and definite, is like *ghulam Zayd* (Zayd's servant), unless you intend the narration of a past state.

*Al-waṣīd* means the courtyard; it was also said the threshold, and it was also said the door. The poet said:

*In a wide land whose waṣīd is not closed to me,*
*and my known [kindness] there is not unrecognized.*

[The poet is Zuhayr. *Al-waṣīd* means the courtyard, the door, and the threshold. He says: I alighted in a land empty of buildings, where guests and wayfarers reach me, having no building with a waṣīd. So it is not closed upon me, and I am hidden from the guests like the people of settled places. Thus the negation of closing is a metaphor for the negation of the waṣīd altogether, and my good conduct there is a known matter that no one among the people denies.]

It was recited as *wa-la-mulli'ta* with the lam doubled for emphasis. It was also recited with the hamza lightened and changed to a ya'. *Ruʿban*, with the ʿayn lightened and heavy, is the fear that fills the chest with dread, that is, fills it, and this is because of the awe that God clothed them in. It was also said: because of the length of their nails and hair and the largeness of their bodies. It was also said: because of the loneliness of their place.

It is reported from Muʿawiya that he raided the Byzantines and passed by the cave, and he said: "If only these people were uncovered for us so we could look at them." Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "That is not for you. God Most High has prevented it from one better than you," and [God] says ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight﴾. Muʿawiya said: "I will not stop until I know their state." So he sent some men and said to them: "Go and look." They did so, and when they entered the cave, God sent a wind upon them and it burned them.

[Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, ʿUbayd ibn Muhammad, and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba, from the narration of Yaʿla ibn Muslim from Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas. Its chain is sound.]

It was recited as *law ittalaʿta* with the waw vocalized with a damma.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verses 19–20:

﴿And thus We raised them up﴾, just as We had made them sleep that sleep. Thus We raised them up as a reminder of His power over both causing sleep and raising from it, so that they might question one another, learn their own state and what God had done with them, take a lesson from it, draw inference about the greatness of God's power, and increase in certainty, and thank God for the blessing He bestowed upon them. ﴿They said: We have remained a day or part of a day﴾: this is an answer based on what is most likely (ghalib al-zann). In it is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) and of speaking on the basis of a predominant opinion, and that this is not a lie, even though it may be an error. ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾: this is a rebuke from some of them to others, and that God knows best the length of their stay. It is as if these people had known, through proofs or through inspiration from God, that the period was long, and that its exact measure was unclear and known only to God.

It is related that they entered the cave in the morning, and their waking was after noon, so they assumed they were still within their same day. When they saw the length of their nails and hair, they said that. If you ask: how did their words ﴿So send one of you﴾ connect with the discussion of the period? I answer: it is as though they said: "Your Lord knows that; you have no means to know it, so turn to something else that concerns you."

Al-waraq means silver, whether minted or unminted. From it is the hadith that Arfajah's nose was struck on the day of al-Kullab [[The phrase "yawm al-Kullab" refers to the battle of al-Kullab, and it is with a dammah: the name of a water-source where the battle took place, as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]], so he made a nose of silver, which then became foul-smelling, and the Messenger of God ﷺ ordered him to make a nose of gold [[Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan from the transmission of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Tarafah, from Arfajah. In another transmission by some, it is "that Arfajah"."]].

It is recited bi-warqikum, with the rāʾ sukūn and the wāw fatḥa or kasra. Ibn Kathir recited bi-warqikum with kasra on the rāʾ and idgham (assimilation) of the qāf into the kāf. It is also related from Ibn Muhaysin that he kasrah the wāw, sukūn the rāʾ and assimilated, but this is not permissible, because of the meeting of two sukūns, and it is not in its proper form.

It has been said that the city was Tarsus. They said: the provision they took with them of silver at the time of their flight is evidence that carrying provisions and what suits the traveller is the view of those who trust in God, as opposed to those who rely on chance and on what is in the purses of people. From this is the statement of ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, to one who asked her about a muhrim (one in the state of ihram) whose money-belt was tied on him: "Tie your provision securely on yourself."[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah with a sound chain from her to this effect.]]

And what is related of some of the poor scholars: he had a strong longing to be granted the pilgrimage to the House of God, and this was known from him. Whenever a group of the wealthy people of his town resolved to perform the Hajj, they came to him, offered to take him with them, and insisted on it. He would excuse himself to them and thank them for their generosity. When they had left him, he would say to those near him: "For this journey there are only two things: tying the money-belt and trusting in the Most Merciful."

﴿Let him look to see which of them is the purest in food﴾: which of its people, the word "people" being omitted, as in His saying ﴿And ask the town﴾; "the purest in food" means the most lawful, best, most abundant and cheapest. ﴿And let him be gentle﴾: let him take care and be diligent in the gentleness and skill of the transaction, so that he is not cheated; or in the matter of concealment, so that he is not recognised. ﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾: that is, let him not do what unintentionally leads to anyone sensing us; that is called making them aware of us, because he is the cause of it. The pronoun in ﴿for they﴾ refers to the "people" implied in ﴿which of them﴾. ﴿If they come upon you they will stone you﴾: they will kill you in the most evil way, which is stoning, as was their custom. ﴿Or they will return you to their religion﴾: by harsh coercion, and make you go back to it. The meaning of "return" (ʿawd) in the sense of "become" is the most common usage in their speech; they say "I no longer do such-and-such," meaning the beginning of the action. ﴿And you will never prosper, then, ever﴾: if you enter their religion.

The pronoun in ﴿for they﴾ refers to the "people" implied in ﴿which of them﴾. ﴿If they come upon you they will stone you﴾: they will kill you in the most evil way, which is stoning, as was their custom. ﴿Or they will return you to their religion﴾: by harsh coercion, and make you go back to it. The meaning of "return" (ʿawd) in the sense of "become" is the most common usage in their speech; they say "I no longer do such-and-such," meaning the beginning of the action. ﴿And you will never prosper, then, ever﴾: if you enter their religion.

And thus We caused them to be discovered, just as We had put them to sleep and raised them up. Because of the wisdom in that, We made them known, so that those to whom We made their condition known would know that the promise of God is true, which is the Resurrection, since their state in their sleep and their waking after it was like the state of one who dies and is then raised. "Idh yatanazi'una" is connected to "a'thar-na" (We caused to be discovered). That is: We caused them to be discovered at the time when they were disputing among themselves the matter of their religion and differing over the reality of the Resurrection. Some of them said: "Only the spirits will be raised, not the bodies." Others said: "The bodies will be raised together with the spirits." So the dispute would be removed, and it would become clear that the bodies will be raised alive and sentient, with their spirits in them, as they were before death. "Faqalu" (they said), when God caused the People of the Cave to die: "Build over them a structure" (bunyanan), that is, over the entrance of their cave, so that people would not reach them, out of concern for their dust and to preserve it, just as the dust of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was preserved by the enclosure. "Those who prevailed over their affair" (alladhina ghalaba 'ala amrihim), from among the Muslims and their rulers, who had more right to them and to building over them, said: "We will surely take over the entrance of the cave a place of worship (masjid)" where Muslims would pray and seek blessing from their place.

It was also said: "Idh yatanazi'una baynahum amrahum" means that people discussed among themselves the matter of the People of the Cave and talked about their story and the sign God had shown concerning them. Or it means they disputed among themselves how to arrange their affair after they died: how should they conceal their place, and how should they block the way to them? So they said: "Build over the entrance of their cave a structure."

It is related that the People of the Gospel had great sins among them, and their kings became tyrannical, until they worshipped idols and were forced to worship them. Among those most insistent on this was Daqyanus. He wanted some youths from the nobles of his people to adopt polytheism and threatened them with death, but they refused except to remain steadfast in faith and firm in it. Then they fled to the cave, and they passed by a dog which followed them, so they drove it away, and God made it speak, and it said: "What do you want from me? I love the beloved of God. Sleep, and I will guard you."

It was also said: they passed by a shepherd with a dog, which followed them "on their religion." They entered the cave and worshipped God there. Then God struck their ears (with sleep). It was also said that before God raised them, the king of their city, a righteous believer, was sent to them. The people of his kingdom had differed about the Resurrection, some acknowledging it and some denying it. So the king entered his house, closed its door, put on a hair shirt, sat on ashes, and asked his Lord to make the truth clear to them. Then God put into the heart of a man among their shepherds to demolish what had been used to block the mouth of the cave, so that he could make it an enclosure for his sheep. When he entered the city, those who had sent him to buy food brought out the silver coins, and that was from the time of Daqyanus. They accused him of having found a treasure, so they took him to the king and related the story to him. The king set out with the people of the city, and they saw them. They praised God for the sign that indicates the Resurrection. Then the youths said to the king: "We entrust you to God, and we seek refuge in Him from the evil of jinn and humans." Then they returned to their resting places, and God took their souls. The king threw his garments over them and ordered that a coffin of gold be made for each of them. But he saw them in a dream disliking gold, so he made them (coffins) of teak, and he built a place of worship over the entrance of the cave.

"Their Lord knows best about them" is from the speech of the disputants, as if they had discussed their affair, exchanged words about their lineages, their conditions, and the length of their stay, and when they could not reach the reality of that, they said: "Their Lord knows best about them." Or it is the speech of God Most High, a rebuttal to the words of those who delved into their story from among those disputants, or from those who disputed about them in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among the People of the Book.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 22:**

﴿They will say [they were three, the fourth of them being their dog]﴾. The pronoun refers to those who disputed about their story during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the believers. They asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about them, and he delayed the answer until it was revealed to him concerning them. So this was revealed as a report of what would take place among them of disagreement about their number, and that the one who is correct among them is the one who says "seven, and the eighth is their dog." Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, said: "I am among that small number."

It is narrated that al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib and their companions, from the people of Najran, were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the mention of the People of the Cave came up. Al-Sayyid, who was a Jacobite, said: "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog." Al-ʿAqib, who was a Nestorian, said: "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog." The Muslims said: "They were seven, and the eighth of them is their dog." So God confirmed the saying of the Muslims.

They knew this only through the report of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him.

It is related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that they were seven men whose names were: Yamlikha, Maksalmina, Mashlīnā (these were the companions of the king's right hand), and on his left: Marnush, Dabarnush, and Shadhnush. He used to consult these six in his affair.

The seventh was the shepherd who joined them when they fled from their king Decius (Daqyanus). The name of their city was Ephesus (Afsus).

The name of their dog was Qiṭmīr.

If you ask: why did the sign of the future (*sīn al-istiqbāl*, the prefix *sa-*) come with the first [saying] and not with the other two? I answer: there are two views on this. One is that the other two fall under the rule of the *sīn*, as you say "he has honoured and bestowed," meaning the sense of expectation applies to both verbs together. The other is that you take the verb in the sense of futurity, which it is capable of bearing: ﴿rajman bil-ghayb﴾, "casting at the unseen," meaning throwing out a hidden report and bringing it forth, like His saying ﴿wa yaqdhūna bil-ghayb﴾ ("and they hurl at the unseen"), i.e., they bring it forth. Or the word *rajm* (casting) is placed in the position of *ẓann* (supposition), as if it had been said: "a supposition about the unseen," because they had so often said "casting at conjecture" in place of "supposing," until for them there was no longer any difference between the two expressions. Do you not see the saying of Zuhayr:

*"And war is nothing but what you have known and tasted,*
*and it is not a conjectured tale told about it."*

This is from his Mu'allaqa, forbidding ʿAbs and Dhubyan from fighting. He says: war is nothing but that which you have known and tried, and he likened it, by way of metaphor and of taste as imagery, to a food that is disliked. *Wa mā huwa* ("and it is not") — that is, the talk about war. Since the pronoun refers in meaning to the verbal noun, the prepositional phrase can be attached to it, and it is far-fetched to attach it to what follows. *Tarjīm* means throwing with pebbles, which are small stones; it is borrowed for uttering speech without deliberation or thought, by way of explicit metaphor.

That is, the supposed [number]. It is also read *thalāthat rābiʿuhum* (with the *tāʾ* of the feminine), with the *thāʾ* assimilated into the *tāʾ* of the feminine. ﴿Thalāthatun﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "they are three." Likewise ﴿khamsatun﴾ and ﴿sabʿatun﴾. ﴿Rābiʿuhum kalbuhum﴾ is a sentence of subject and predicate standing as an adjective of ﴿thalāthatun﴾; likewise ﴿sādisuhum kalbuhum﴾ and ﴿thāminuhum kalbuhum﴾.

If you ask: what is this *waw* that enters the third sentence, and why did it enter it and not the first two? [Mahmud said: "If you say: why did the *waw* enter the last sentence...?" Ahmad said: "This is the correct view, unlike those who say that it is the *waw* of eight (*wāwu al-thamāniya*), for that is a matter that does not hold firm for its proponent. They count with this *waw* the words in His saying concerning Paradise, ﴿wa futihat abwābuhā﴾ ("and its gates were opened"), in contrast to the gates of Hell, for He said of them ﴿futihat abwābuhā﴾ without the *waw*. They said: because the gates of Paradise are eight, and the gates of Hell are seven. But even granting that there is in the language a *waw* that accompanies the eighth and is specific to it, where is the mention of a number in the gates of Paradise so that it reaches the eighth and is accompanied by the *waw*? And they sometimes count among these ﴿wa'l-nāhūna ʿani'l-munkar﴾ ("and those who forbid wrong"), which is the eighth in His saying ﴿al-tā'ibūna﴾ ("those who repent"). This too is rejected, for the *waw* is only attached to this attribute in order to link it to the first, which is ﴿al-āmirūna bil-maʿrūf﴾ ("those who enjoin right"), because of the connection and linkage between them. Do you not see their being joined in all their sources and occurrences, as in His saying ﴿yaʾmurūna bil-maʿrūfi wa yanhawna ʿani'l-munkar﴾ ("they enjoin right and forbid wrong") and His saying ﴿wa'mur bil-maʿrūfi wa'nha ʿani'l-munkar﴾ ("enjoin right and forbid wrong")? Some have also counted among these the *waw* in His saying ﴿thayyibātin wa abkāran﴾ ("previously married and virgins"), because they found it with the eighth, but this is a gross error, for this is the *waw* of division (*wāw al-taqsīm*). If you were to remove it and say ﴿thayyibātin abkāran﴾, the sentence would not hold together. It is therefore clear that the *waw* in all these enumerated places is used for something other than what these people claimed. And God is the Granter of success."]? I answer: it is the *waw* that enters a sentence which is an adjective of an indefinite noun, as it enters a sentence which is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of a definite noun, as in your saying: "A man came to me and with him another," and "I passed by Zayd and in his hand was a sword." And from it His saying the Exalted: ﴿wa mā ahlaknā min qaryatin illā wa lahā kitābun maʿlūm﴾ ("We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree"). Its purpose is to emphasize the adhesion of the attribute to the thing described, and to indicate that its being characterized by it is a established and firm matter. This *waw* is the one that gave notice that those who said "seven, and the eighth is their dog" spoke from firm knowledge and tranquillity of soul, and did not cast at the unseen as the others did. The proof of this is that God, glorified is He, followed the first two sayings with His words ﴿rajman bil-ghayb﴾, and followed the third saying with His words ﴿mā yaʿlamuhum illā qalīl﴾ ("none knows them except a few").

Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, said: "When the *waw* came, the count ended," that is, no counter remained after it to whom one would pay attention. It is established that they were seven, and their eighth was their dog, with certainty and confirmation.

It is also said: "except a few of the People of the Book." On this view the pronoun in ﴿sa-yaqūlūna﴾ refers to the People of the Book specifically, meaning: "the People of the Book will say such and such about them, and there is no knowledge of that except among a few of them, while most of them are speaking by conjecture and guesswork."

﴿So do not dispute about them﴾, that is, do not argue with the People of the Book concerning the matter of the Companions of the Cave, except with an apparent argument not carried to excess, which is that you relate to them only what God has revealed to you, and add nothing, without ignorance-attributing to them or harshness toward them in refuting them, as He said: ﴿and argue with them in the best manner﴾. ﴿And do not ask for a verdict﴾, that is, do not ask any of them about their story with the question of one who seeks to trouble them, until he says something that you can reject and show to be false from what he has, because that contradicts what you were enjoined concerning gentleness and courtesy; nor with the question of one who seeks guidance, because God has already guided you by revealing their story to you.

And do not say of anything, "I shall certainly do that tomorrow," [or: "do not say for the sake of anything"] — that is, in what is to come in time — and he did not specify tomorrow in particular — except [when] God wills. The clause "except that God wills" is connected to the prohibition, not to his saying "I shall do," because if he had said, "I shall do such-and-such, unless God wills," its meaning would be: unless the will of God intervenes to prevent his doing it, and that has no bearing on the prohibition. Its connection to the prohibition has two possible readings. The first: "Do not say that statement except that God wills that you say it, by permitting you to do so." The second: "Do not say it except by God's will," i.e., except by the will of God, and this is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: except while joined with God's will, saying, "If God wills." There is also a third possibility: that "except that God wills" carries the sense of an expression of permanence, as if it were said, "do not say it ever." Similar to it is His saying: "It is not for us to return to it, except that God wills" (7:89), because their returning to their creed is something God will never will.

This is a prohibition from God, as a form of discipline for His Prophet, when the Jews said to the Quraysh: "Ask him about the spirit, about the People of the Cave, and about Dhu al-Qarnayn." They asked him, and he said: "Come to me tomorrow and I will inform you," and he did not add the exception. The revelation was delayed until it weighed heavily upon him, and the Quraysh denied him. "And remember your Lord" — that is, the will of your Lord — and say, "If God wills," when you have forgotten it. The meaning is: if you forget the word of exception and then become aware of it, make up for it by mentioning it. He said: "And His saying, 'and remember your Lord when you forget' — that is, the word of exception — then you become aware of it, and make up for it by mentioning it."

From Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him): "Even after a year, so long as you have not broken the oath." From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Even after a day, or a week, or a month, or a year." From Tawus: "It is valid as its exception (thunya) so long as he remains in his session." (The Sihah defines "thunya," with a damma, as the noun of istithna'.) Similarly from al-Hasan. From 'Ata': "He may make the exception for the length of time it takes to milk a copious she-camel."

According to the majority of jurists, the exception has no effect on the rulings unless it is connected (to the statement). It is related that news reached al-Mansur that Abu Hanifa differed from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him) concerning the detached exception, so he summoned him to rebuke him. Abu Hanifa said: "This rebounds upon you: you take the pledge of allegiance by oaths. Would you be content that they leave your presence and make an exception, and so escape from you?" He found his words admirable and was pleased with him.

It may also be that the meaning is: "And remember your Lord" — by glorifying Him and seeking His forgiveness — when you forget the word of exception, as an emphasis on giving it attention. It was also said: "Remember your Lord when you have abandoned some of what He commanded you." And it was said: "Remember Him when forgetfulness overtakes you, so that He may remind you of what was forgotten," and it has been interpreted as referring to performing a forgotten prayer when one remembers it.

"And say: It may be that my Lord will guide me to something nearer than this in rectitude" — this refers to the account of the People of the Cave. The meaning: may God give me clearer signs and proofs that I am a truthful prophet, which are greater in indication and closer to rectitude than the account of the People of the Cave. He did so, granting him accounts of the prophets and reports of the unseen greater and more demonstrative than that. The apparent meaning is: if you forget something, remember your Lord.

Remembering your Lord when you forget is to say: "It may be that my Lord will guide me to something other than this forgotten matter, nearer to rectitude (rashadan) and better in benefit and profit." Perhaps the forgetting was itself a good choice, as in His saying: "Or We cause it to be forgotten, and We bring one better than it" (2:106).

And they remained in their cave three hundred years. "Yielding" means that their staying alive in it during this period was (the meaning of) "We had struck upon their ears in the cave for a number of years" (18:11), which is an explanation of what was stated in summary there. As for the words "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained" (18:26), the meaning is that He knows better than those who disputed about them the duration of their stay, and the truth is what Allah has told you. It is related from Qatadah that this is a report of the speech of the People of the Book, and "Say: Allah knows best" is a rejoinder to them. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "And they said: They remained..."

"Years" (sinin) is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "three hundred." It is also read as "three hundred years" with the genitive construction (idafah), placing the plural in the position of the singular after the specifier (tamyiz), as in His words "the greatest losers in deeds" (bi-l-akhsarina aʿmalan) (18:103). In the reading of Ubayy it is "three hundred years" (sanah). "Nine" (tis'an) means nine years, because what precedes it indicates it. Al-Hasan read it as "tis'an" with a fatha.

Then He mentions His exclusive knowledge of what is hidden in the heavens and the earth and what is concealed in them of the conditions of their inhabitants and of others, and that He alone has knowledge of it. He brought (this statement) with what indicates amazement at His perception of what is heard and what is seen, to show that His perception is beyond the limit of the perception of hearers and seers, for He perceives the most subtle and smallest things just as He perceives the largest in bulk and densest in substance, and He perceives the inner as He perceives the outer. "They have" (lahum): the pronoun refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. "No guardian" (min waliyyin): one who manages their affairs. "And He does not make anyone a partner in His judgment" (wa la yushriku fi hukmihi ahadan): in His decree, anyone among them. Al-Hasan read it as "wa la tushrik," with a ta' and a jazm, as a prohibition (nahy).

They were saying to him: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." So it was said to him: "Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book (al-Qur'an), and do not heed their babbling about seeking a substitution. There is no one who can alter the words of your Lord," i.e., no one can be capable of changing or altering them; He alone has that power. "And when We substitute one verse in place of another..." "And you will never find, other than Him, a refuge" (multaḥad), a place of refuge you could turn to if you were to resolve upon that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 28:

Some of the chiefs of the disbelievers said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Push away these clients, whose smell is like the smell of sheep: they are Suhayb, 'Ammar, Khabbab and others among the poor Muslims, so that we may sit with you, as the people of Noah said: ﴿Shall we believe you, when the lowest of the people follow you?﴾ [Q. 26:111]." So the verse was revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself along with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [Q. 18:28]. That is, hold yourself back and keep yourself firm with them. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*So I endured, knowing for it, a firm one, steady when the frightened soul strains forward.*

[On Abu Dhu'ayb's elegy for his sons. "Endured" (ṣabartu) means: I held back a soul that knew that affliction. He made 'ārifa ("knowing") carry the sense of "enduring" (ṣābira), so he construed it with the preposition lām. Jasra means strong and hard. Another reading is ḥurra, with a ḥā' bearing a ḍammah, meaning "excellent." Tarsū means: is at rest and calm, while the soul of the coward strains forward (tatallaʿ) and grows anxious, as if it wants to flee. The original form is tatatallaʿ, from which one of the two tā's was dropped for lightness.]

*Morning and evening*: persistent in supplication at every time. It is said that what is meant is the dawn and the afternoon prayers. It is read as *bil-ghadwa* ("in the morning"), but *bil-ghadāt* is better, because *ghadwa* is used as a proper noun in most usage. Placing the definite article *al-* on it is in the sense of indefiniteness, as in the line:

*...and Zayd, the Zayd of the battlefields*

[The line: "Among them were Hajib and the son of his mother, Abu Jundal, and Zayd, the Zayd of the battlefields." Here the definite article *al-* was placed on "Zayd," which is a proper name, because it is construed as "one named Zayd," and for this reason he was made to govern *al-ma'ārik* ("the battlefields"), that is, the places of wars. The poet says: among these people was Hajib ibn Laqit ibn Zurara, and the son of his mother, that is his brother Abu Jundal, and the one named Yazid, who was prepared for wars. This contains an indication that he was known by this among the people.]

Such use is rare in their speech. One says *'adāhu* ("he passed him by") when he goes beyond him, and from this come their expressions *'adā ṭawrahu* ("he exceeded his limit") and *jā'anī al-qawmu 'adā Zaydan* ("the people came to me, excluding Zayd"). It is construed with *'an* only because *'adā* is made to carry the meaning of *nabā* ("to turn away") and *'alā* ("to rise above"), as in your saying *nabat 'anhu 'aynuhu* ("his eye turned away from him") and *'alat 'anhu 'aynuhu* ("his eye rose above him"), when one storms past something without holding fast to it. If you ask: what is the purpose of this inclusion? Why not say: "let not your eyes pass over them," or "let not your eyes rise above them"? I answer: its purpose is to give the combined sense of both meanings, and that is stronger than giving a single meaning alone. Do you not see how the meaning returns to your saying: "let not your eyes storm over them, passing beyond them to others"? Similar to it is the saying of God: ﴿And do not devour their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [Q. 4:2], meaning: do not add it to your wealth while devouring it.

It is also read *wa lā tuʿid 'aynayka* and *wa lā tuʿadd 'aynayka*, from *a'dāhu* and *'addāhu*, with transitivity by the prefix *hamza* and by doubling the middle letter. From this is the line:

*So turn away from what you see, for there is no return for it, and fasten the saddle-frames upon a swift, hard she-camel.*

[This is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani. *Nama yanmī namyan* means: it increased and rose. *Namāhu yanmīhi namyan* means: he raised it and increased it. *Nama yanmū numuwwan* is from the category *dakhala*. *Namāhu yanmūhu numuwwan* is also used, but the form from the root with *wāw* is rare. The *qutūd* (saddle-frames) are the plural of *aqtād*, which is the plural of *qatad*, meaning wooden frames of the saddle without its fittings. *Al-ʿayrāna* is the one resembling the wild ass in speed of travel. *Al-ajad* is the hard, firmly built one. He says: turn away from what you see of the traces of dwellings, or from what you expect to return, for there is no overtaking of it and no return to it, and raise the saddle-frames upon a swift, hard she-camel. This is a metaphor for ordering him to travel, because the fastening of riding-gear belongs only to the journey.] Its meaning is: *fa-ʿudda hammaka ʿammā tarā*, "turn your concern away from what you see."

The Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden to look down on the poor believers, and to let his eye turn away from the shabbiness of their dress out of longing for the dress of the rich and the fineness of their appearance. [Al-Zamakhshari's words "and the fineness of their appearance": in the *Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): *al-shiwār* and *al-shāra* are clothing and appearance. (ʿ)]

﴿Desiring the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [Q. 18:28]: this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). ﴿Whose heart We have made heedless﴾: whose heart We made heedless. [Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: We made his heart heedless of the remembrance... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This tends toward fleeing from the truth, namely that the intended meaning is that We created it for him, and it is fitting that it should tend toward following his desire. If "made heedless" (*aghfalnā*) is taken on its own pattern, it is directed to abandonment (*khidhlān*); otherwise it must be taken entirely out of its pattern into the pattern of *af'ala* for coincidence. One should not presume to interpret a verb which God attributes to Himself as coincidence, which conveys the finding of a thing suddenly after prior ignorance and lack of knowledge.] ﴿Of the remembrance﴾, by abandonment. [Al-Zamakhshari's words "heedless of the remembrance by abandonment" shy away from attributing heedlessness to God's creation of his heart, because God does not create evil according to the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school), while the Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni majority) hold otherwise, as he indicates by saying: "the Jabriyya (determinists) imagine..." Moreover, his following his desire does not contradict God's creating heedlessness in his heart, since it is possible that this arises from heedlessness. (ʿ)]

Or: We found him heedless of it, as you say: *ajbantuhu* ("I found him a coward"), *afḥamtuhu* ("I found him unable to speak"), and *abkhaltuhu* ("I found him stingy"), when you find him to be so. Or: from *aghfala ibilahu*, when he left his camels without a mark, meaning: we did not mark him with remembrance, and we did not make him one of those in whose hearts We have written faith. [Al-Zamakhshari's continuation: "It may also be that the meaning is: from *aghfala ibilahu* when..." Ahmad said: This interpretation has a delicate subtlety and a refined meaning, and his purpose in it is to escape what we have already mentioned, because although he refuses that God creates heedlessness in the heart, he does not refuse the absence of the writing of faith. Our aim is only to point out that al-Zamakhshari's intention is to turn away from the principle stated earlier. Interpretation is resorted to only when the apparent meaning is impossible, and for us the apparent meaning is possible, so it is obligatory to hold fast to it. And God grants success.] ﴿And he followed his desire﴾ [Q. 18:28]: God has refuted the imagination of the Jabriyya by this statement. [Al-Zamakhshari's continuation: "God has refuted the imagination of the Jabriyya by saying: 'and he followed his desire.'" Ahmad said: It has already been mentioned in more than one place that the Ahl al-Sunna attribute the act of the servant to God insofar as it is created by Him, and to the servant insofar as it is conjoined with his power and choice. There is no contradiction between the two attributions, and the proofs of the Sunna follow him wherever he goes and in whatever direction he turns, so he has no escape from them in any way.]

It is also read *aghfalnā qalbahu*, with the verb attributed to the heart, in the sense: "We found his heart heedless," from *aghfaltuhu*, when I found him heedless.

﴿And his affair has been ﻓُرُطاً﴾ [Q. 18:28]: going beyond the truth and the right. [Al-Zamakhshari's words "going beyond the truth and the right": that is, one who precedes it and transgresses it. In the *Sihah*: *amrun furuṭun* means an affair in which one exceeds the limit. From this is God's saying: ﴿and his affair was furuṭ﴾ [Q. 33:38]. Casting it aside behind his back, from the saying "a *faras furuṭ*," a horse that precedes other horses.]

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 29:**

﴿And say: "The truth is from your Lord."﴾ Al-ḥaqq is the predicate of an elided subject (khabar mubtada' maḥdhūf). The meaning is: the truth has come and the pretexts have been removed [[His saying "the meaning is: the truth has come and the pretexts have been removed": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "zāḥa al-shay'" means it passed away and departed; "azaḥtu 'illatahu fa-zāḥat" means I removed his ailment and it was removed. (Ṭ.)]], so nothing remains except your choosing for yourselves whatever you wish: to take the path of salvation or the path of destruction. The imperative and the language of choice are used because, since He has enabled you to choose whichever of the two you wish, you are as one who is given the choice and commanded to choose whatever he wills from the two highways.

﴿The fire, whose enclosure surrounds them.﴾ The fire that encompasses them is likened to the sarādiq, which is the enclosure that stands around the tent (fusṭāṭ), and "bayt musarduq" means a house with a sarādiq. It is said: it is a smoke that encompasses the disbelievers before they enter the fire. And it is said: it is a wall of fire that circles them [[His saying "yuṭīfu bihim" (circles them): what al-Ṣiḥāḥ indicates is: "ṭāfa yaṭūfu ḥawla al-shay'" means he went around it, and "ṭāfa yuṭīfu bi-al-shay'" means he came to it and afflicted him. Reflect. (Ṭ.)]].

﴿If they ask for relief, they will be given water like molten metal, which scalds the faces.﴾ This is like the saying of the poet: "...... so they were recompensed with the Ṣaylam" [[The explanation of this witness was given in the first volume, p. 105, so refer to it if you wish. (Its editor.)]], and there is mockery in it. Al-muhl is what has been melted from the substances of the earth. And it is said: it is the dregs of oil, which scorches the faces; when it is brought near to drink, the face is scorched by its heat. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is like the dregs of oil." [[Al-Tirmidhi narrated it through the route of Rushdin ibn Sa'd, from 'Amr ibn al-Ḥārith, from Darrāj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id. He considered it strange and said: it is not known except from the hadith of Rushdin ibn Sa'd. His statement was criticised: Aḥmad and Abu Ya'lā narrated it through the route of Ibn Lahī'ah from Darrāj, and Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim narrated it through the route of Ibn Wahb from 'Amr ibn al-Ḥārith.]] When it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off.

﴿Wretched is the drink, and evil is the fire as a resting place.﴾ Murtafaqan means a couch (muttaka) from the elbow (al-mirfaq). This is for the sake of matching His saying ﴿and good is the resting place (murtafaqan)﴾; otherwise there is no reclining (irtifāq) for the people of the fire nor leaning, unless it is from the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I stayed awake, and spent the night reclining on the elbow, as though in my eyes is the bitter aloe, slaughtered." [[By Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali. It is also narrated with the first hemistich replaced by: "maqām al-khalī wa bitta al-layla mashtajiran." Al-irtifāq: leaning on the elbow with the forearm raised. Al-ishtijār: placing the hand under the jaw, between the two cheeks, and leaning on it, which is the posture of one who grieves and is distressed. Al-araq: sleeplessness. Al-ṣāb: a bitter plant like the colocynth. Al-madhbūḥ: the split, which is a metaphor for weeping and the flowing of tears.]]

Ulā'ika (those) is the predicate of inna (indeed), and innā lā nuḍī' (indeed We do not waste) is a parenthetical interjection (i'tirāḍ). It is also permissible to make innā lā nuḍī' and ulā'ika two predicates together. Or you may make ulā'ika a separate, resumed sentence (kalām mustaʾnaf), explaining the reward that was left vague.

If you say: when you take innā lā nuḍī' as the predicate, where is the pronoun returning from it to the subject? I say: man aḥsana ʿamalan (whoever does good deeds) and alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt (those who believe and do righteous deeds) are joined by a single meaning, so man aḥsana took the place of the pronoun. Or you may intend: "whoever among them does better in deeds," and this is like your saying: "Butter is two ratls for a dirham." Here min (from) in the first instance denotes the beginning (ibtidāʾ), and the second min denotes specification (tabyīn).

The indefiniteness of asāwira (bracelets) is for the purpose of leaving its excellence undefined. He combined sundus (fine silk, the thinner part of brocade) and istabraq (thick brocade), combining the two kinds. He singled out reclining (al-ittikāʾ) because it is the posture of the privileged and of kings upon their couches.

And strike for them an example of two men. That is: the likeness of the disbelievers and the believers, compared to the condition of two men, and they were two brothers among the Children of Israel: one of them a disbeliever named Qatrus, and the other a believer named Yahudha. It was also said:

They are the two referred to in Surat al-Saffat in His saying ﴿A speaker among them will say: "Indeed, I had a companion"﴾. They inherited eight thousand dinars from their father, and divided them between themselves. The disbeliever bought land for a thousand, and the believer said: "O Allah, my brother has bought land for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand," and he gave it in charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I have made a thousand a dowry for the maidens (ḥūr)." Then his brother bought servants and goods for a thousand, and he said: "O Allah, I have bought from You the everlasting youths for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then he came to need, so he sat on the road of his brother; when his brother passed by him with his retinue, he approached him, and he drove him away and rebuked him for giving away his wealth. It was also said:

They are a likeness of two brothers from the Banu Makhzum: a believer, who was Abu Salamah, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, who had been the husband of Umm Salamah before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); and a disbeliever, who was al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad.

﴿Two gardens of grapevines﴾: two orchards of vines. ﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: We made the palms encircle the two gardens. This is something that the landowners (dahāqīn, sing. dahqān) prefer for their vineyards: that they be fringed with fruit-bearing trees. It is said: ḥafaw-hu, when they went around it, and ḥaffaytu-hu bihim, meaning: I made them encircle it. The verb is transitive to one object, and then the bāʾ makes it take a second object, as in your saying ghashiyahu and ghashaytuhu bihi. ﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: We made them a land comprising foodstuffs and fruits. He described the cultivation as continuous and interlaced, with no intervening thing cutting it off or separating it, together with a good form and an elegant arrangement; and He described them as yielding their fruits fully, without any shortfall in the produce. Then [He mentioned] the thing that is the root and source of good, namely the matter of irrigation, and made it the best of what they are watered with, which is flowing water from a river running through them.

And al-akl (the produce) means the fruit. It was read with a ḍammah on the kāf (ukul). ﴿And did not wrong﴾: did not lack or diminish. ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce (ātat)﴾: the verb agrees with the wording, since kilā (both) has the form of a singular word; had it been said ātatā according to the meaning, that would also be permissible. It was read wa-fajjarnā with the lightened form. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) read kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu, referring the pronoun back to kull. ﴿And he had fruit﴾: that is, kinds of wealth, from the fruit of his property, when it increased. It is related from Mujahid: gold and silver, meaning that he had, in addition to the two gardens described, abundant wealth in gold and silver and other things, and he was affluent in every respect, able to cultivate the land as he willed. ﴿And he had more support in men﴾: meaning more helpers and retinue. It was also said: more male children, because they go forth with him, unlike females. ﴿Yuhāwiruhu﴾: he would enter into discussion with him, from ḥāra yaḥūru, meaning he returned; and I asked him, but he did not return a word (mā aḥāra kalimah).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verses 35–36:

It means: Qitrus took his fellow, the Muslim, by the hand, walking him around the two gardens, showing him what was in them, impressing him with them, and boasting to him of the wealth he possessed apart from him. If you say: why did he single out "the garden" after the dual form? I say: the meaning is "and he entered his garden, which was all he had, he had no garden other than it." That is, he has no share in the Garden promised to the believers; what he possessed in this world is his garden and nothing else. He did not intend the two gardens, nor either of them. "And he was wronging himself" [18:35]: he was pleased with what he had been given, proud of it, and ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord, thereby exposing himself to the wrath of God, and this is the most heinous wrong.

His report about himself, expressing doubt about the perishing of his garden, is due to his long hope, the domination of greed over him, the prolongation of his heedlessness, his being deceived by the respite, and his neglect of considering the outcomes of people like him. You will find most wealthy Muslims, even if they do not utter anything like this with their tongues, their conditions speak it and proclaim it. "And if I am returned to my Lord" [18:36]: this is an oath from him that, supposing he were returned to his Lord, as his companion claims, he would surely find in the Hereafter something better than his garden in this world, out of presumption and wishful thinking regarding God, and claiming honor in His sight and a standing with Him, and that He gave him the two gardens only because of his deserving and worthiness, and that this deserving accompanies him wherever he turns, like his saying: "If there is for me with Him indeed the best [reward]" [41:50], "I will surely be given wealth and children" [19:77]. It has also been read "khayran minhuma" (better than them both), as a response to the two gardens. "Better in return (munqalaban)": in outcome and consequence.

Its accusative case is as a specification (tamyiz): that is, the return of that is better than the return of this, because this is perishing and that is everlasting.
