"And if I am returned to my Lord" [18:36]: this is an oath from him that, supposing he were returned to his Lord, as his companion claims, he would surely find in the Hereafter something better than his garden in this world, out of presumption and wishful thinking regarding God, and claiming honor in His sight and a standing with Him, and that He gave him the two gardens only because of his deserving and worthiness, and that this deserving accompanies him wherever he turns, like his saying: "If there is for me with Him indeed the best [reward]" [41:50], "I will surely be given wealth and children" [19:77]. It has also been read "khayran minhuma" (better than them both), as a response to the two gardens. "Better in return (munqalaban)": in outcome and consequence.

Its accusative case is as a specification (tamyiz): that is, the return of that is better than the return of this, because this is perishing and that is everlasting.

He created you from dust: that is, He created your origin, since the creation of your origin is the cause of your creation, so creating it amounts to creating you. He proportioned you: He made you balanced and perfected you as a man, a male who had reached maturity and the stage of men. He made him a disbeliever in God, one who denies His favors, because of his doubt about the resurrection (al-ba'th), just as one who denies the Messenger (ﷺ) is a disbeliever.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 38:

The original form is "lakinna ana" (but I). The hamza of "ana" was dropped and its vowel placed on the nun of "lakinna," so the two nuns came together and were assimilated (idgham). A similar example is the words of the poet:

"And you shoot me with your glance, meaning you are guilty, and you forsake me; but, by you, I do not forsake you."

[[He says: "And you shoot me," O beloved, with your glance, that is, you direct it at me. So "shooting" is an explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah), since the release of the glance is likened to the release of a stone. It is also permissible that the bā' is instrumental (li-l-alah), in which case the object of shooting is omitted and explained by his words "meaning you are guilty," so that "ay" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), meaning that what she shot him with is her claim that he is guilty. "Qalahu yaqlihi" and "qalihahu yaqlahu" are both used. It may be said that "qalahu yaqlahu" means to hate intensely, but its original form is "wa-lakin ana," where the vowel of the hamza was moved to the nun and then the hamza was dropped; then the nun was assimilated into the following nun, and the final alif is dropped in writing as in pronunciation. If pause were treated as continuation, it would remain. The object, "iyyaka" (you), is placed first for emphasis on clearing her of hating him and for singling her out from other women.]]

That is: "But I do not hate you," where "huwa" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), the matter being "Allah is my Lord," and the clause is the predicate of "ana," and the returning pronoun in it to him is the ya' of the possessive pronoun.

Ibn 'Amir recited with the alif of "ana" affirmed in both pause and continuation, and this is justified by the alif standing as a substitute for the dropped hamza. Others affirm it only in pause. It is related from Abu 'Amr that he paused with the ha': "lakinhu." It has also been read: "lakin huwa Allahu rabbi," with the nun unvowelled and "ana" omitted. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "lakin ana" in its original form. In the reading of 'Abdullah: "lakin ana la ilaha illa huwa rabbi."

If you ask: for what is "huwa" a contrast (istidrak)?

I answer: it is in response to his words, "Do you disbelieve?" He said to his companion: "You are a disbeliever in Allah, but I am a believer who affirms God's oneness," just as you say: "Zayd is absent, but 'Amr is present."

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 18, verses 39–41:**

﴿مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ (﴿What God wills [comes to pass]﴾) may be a *mawsula* (relative pronoun, "that which"), in the nominative position as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence), with the sense: "The matter is what God wills." Or it may be a *shartiyya* (conditional particle), in the accusative position, with its response omitted, meaning: "Whatever thing God wills, it happens." Its counterpart in omitting the response is the *law* (if) in His saying ﴿and if a Qur'an were such that mountains were moved by it...﴾.

The meaning is: when you entered your garden and looked at what God had granted you from it, you should have said, "What God wills [comes to pass]," acknowledging that it and every good in it came about by God's will and grace, and that its affair is in His hand: if He wills, He leaves it flourishing, and if He wills, He ruins it. You should also have said ﴿There is no power except in God﴾, affirming that whatever strength you have to cultivate it and manage its affairs is only by His help and support, since no one has strength in his body or in what his hand possesses except by God, exalted is He.

It is related from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that he would breach his orchard wall during the days of the dates harvest, so that whoever wished could enter. Whenever he entered it, he would repeat this verse until he left.

Whoever reads ﴿aqalla﴾ (less) in the accusative has made ﴿anā﴾ (I) a *fasl* (separating pronoun between the two parts of the sentence). Whoever reads it in the nominative has made it a *mubtada'* (subject), with ﴿aqalla﴾ as its *khabar* (predicate), and the whole clause as the second object (*maf'ul*).

Secondly, ﴿tarani﴾ (you see me). In His saying ﴿and children﴾ there is support for those who interpret *nafar* (group/followers) in His saying ﴿and more powerful in manpower﴾ as "children." The meaning is: if you see me as poorer than you in wealth and children, then I hope from God's action that He will reverse what is between me and you of poverty and wealth, so that He grants me, for my faith, a garden better than your garden, and strips you of His blessing for your disbelief and ruins your orchard.

*Ḥusbān* (reckoning/calamity) is a verbal noun like *ghufrān* (forgiveness) and *buṭlān* (nullity), meaning "reckoning," i.e., a measure God has decreed and reckoned, which is the judgment to ruin it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a punishment of *ḥusbān*, and that *ḥusbān* is the reckoning of what your hands have earned. It is also said that *ḥusbānan* means projectiles, the singular being *ḥusbāna*, which are thunderbolts. ﴿A smooth ground (ṣa'īdan zalaqan)﴾: land that is white, upon which one slips because of its smoothness and slipperiness.

﴿Ghawran﴾ (sunken): both of these words are described by the verbal noun (*maṣdar*).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verses 42–43:

﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾ is an expression for his destruction. Its origin is from "the enemy encompassed him" (ahāṭa bihi al-ʿaduww), because when an enemy encompasses someone, he has taken possession of him and gained control over him. It was then used for every kind of destruction. From this is the words of God, ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ (Yusuf 12:66). Similar to it is their saying: "atā ʿalayhi" (it came upon him), meaning he destroyed him, as in "the enemy came upon them," meaning he came to them overpowering them.

﴿Turning over his palms﴾ is a kināya (figurative expression) for regret and anguish, because the one who regrets turns his palms over, from back to front. Similarly, some of the Arabs expressed this with "biting the hand" (ʿaḍḍ al-kaff) and "falling into the hand" (al-suqūṭ fī al-yad). Because it has the sense of regret, it is construed with ʿalā, as if it were said: ﴿then he began to regret over what he had spent on it﴾, meaning what he had spent on its cultivation, ﴿while it was fallen down upon its trellises﴾, meaning that its vines which were trellised had their trellises collapsed onto the ground, and the vines fell upon them.

It is said: God sent a fire upon it and it consumed it. ﴿Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾. He realised that the calamity had come to him because of his polytheism and his arrogance, so he wished that he had not been a polytheist, so that God would not have destroyed his garden. It is also permissible that this be repentance from polytheism, remorse for what he had done, and entry into faith.

It was recited as ﴿and there was not﴾ with both the yāʾ and the tāʾ. The verb ﴿they will help him﴾ is construed according to the meaning rather than the wording, like the words of God: ﴿a company fighting in the way of God, and another disbelieving, who see them﴾ (Al ʿImran 3:13).

If you say: What is the meaning of His words ﴿they will help him, apart from God﴾? I say: its meaning is that they would be able to help him apart from God; that is, He alone is capable of helping him, and no one other than Him can help him. But He did not help him because of a deterrent, which is that it was due that he be forsaken. ﴿And he was not one who could defend himself﴾, meaning he was not one who could protect himself by his strength from the vengeance of God.

The verb is "wilaya" (guardianship/authority) with a fatha on the first letter... Let me translate directly.

Al-Wilaya, with a fatha, means support and taking charge (al-nusra wa-al-tawalli). With a kasra, it means authority and sovereignty (al-sultan wa-al-mulk). Both have been read. The meaning is: "There" (hunalika), that is, in that station and that situation, support belongs to God alone. No one possesses it and no one is able to give it except Him. This confirms His words ﴿and he had no company to support him against God﴾. Or: "There" sovereignty and dominion belong to God; none can overcome Him or escape from Him. Or: in such a severe situation, every person in distress turns to God and believes in Him. That is, His words ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾ are a statement that he was compelled to say out of distress at the calamity that befell him because of his disbelief; had it not been for that, he would not have said it.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "There, guardianship belongs to God," by which He gives victory to His believing friends over the disbelievers and avenges them and heals their hearts from their enemies. That is, He gave victory, in what He did to the disbeliever, to his believing brother, and confirmed his words ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a punishment from heaven﴾. His words support this: ﴿Better in reward and better in outcome﴾, that is, for His friends. It has also been said that "there" refers to the Hereafter: in that abode, guardianship belongs to God, like His words ﴿To whom belongs sovereignty today?﴾.

The word "al-haqq" has been read in the nominative and the genitive, as an adjective of "al-wilaya" and of "Allah."

[[Mahmud said: "It was read in the nominative and genitive as an adjective of al-wilaya, and of Allah, the Exalted..." etc.]] Ahmad says: Objection has already been raised to such a statement, since it gives the impression that the recitations are left to the judgment of eloquent speakers and the effort of skilled orators, so that they differ in eloquence according to their differing abilities in it. This is a reprehensible and grave error. The truth is that no one may recite except what he has heard and memorized, transmitted by an unbroken chain to the Prophet (ﷺ), revealed thus from heaven. The eloquence of the eloquent therefore carries no weight; he is merely a transmitter like others. Yet al-Zamakhshari does not forgo praising the head of innovation and the source of discord, for ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd was the first to insist on denying divine decree, and so on through all the Mu'tazilite innovations. For this reason he praised him.

ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read "al-haqq" in the accusative as an emphatic, as in your saying: "This is ʿAbd Allah, the truth, not the falsehood." This is a good and eloquent reading, and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd was among the most eloquent and sincere of people.

"ʿUqban" has been read with a damma and with a sukun on the qaf, and "ʿuqbā" on the pattern of "fuʿlā." All of them mean "the outcome" (al-ʿaqiba).

Then the plants of the earth became intermingled with it, thickening and growing dense until some of it was mixed with other parts. It was also said: the water sank into the plants, so they mixed with it until they became lush and glistening, [[His saying "wa-rafa rafifan" — in al-Sihah: "rafa lawnuhu rafan and rafifan" means it shone and sparkled. A "shajar rafif" is a tree whose leaves are moist. (Ibn al-Mundhir? — marginal note)]] and on this interpretation the wording should have been: "fa-ikhtalata bi-nabat al-ard" (the plants of the earth became intermingled). Its soundness is that each of two things mixed is described by the attribute of the other.

Al-hashim: what has been crushed and broken into pieces; its singular is hashima. It is also read "tadhruhu al-rih" (the wind scatters it). From Ibn ʿAbbas: "tadhriyhi al-riyah," from adhra (to scatter). It likens the state of the worldly life in its freshness and splendour, and the destruction and perishing that follow it, to the state of a plant that is green and luxuriant, then dries up and the winds scatter it as if it had never been. [[His saying "bi-hal al-nabat yakunu akhdar wariefan" — in al-Sihah: "warifa al-nabt," meaning it trembled from its freshness, so it is warif, that is, fresh, quivering, and very green. (Marginal note)]] ﴿And God is ever Able over all things﴾, [in creating and in annihilating].

The enduring good deeds (al-Baqiyat al-Salihat): these are the acts of goodness whose fruit remains for a person and passes away from him, [unlike] everything his soul aspires to of the portions of this world. It was also said: they are the five daily prayers. It was said: "Glory be to Allah, all praise is due to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest." And from Qatadah: "Whatever is done seeking the Face of Allah is good ﴿in reward and better in hope﴾." That is: what is connected to them of reward, and what is connected to them of hope, because their doer hopes in this world for the reward of Allah, and attains it in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 47–48:

It is read: "tusayyar" (﴿تُسَيَّرُ﴾), from sayyara (causative), and "nusayyar" (﴿نُسَيِّرُ﴾), from sayyarnā. And "tasīr" (﴿تَسِيرُ﴾), from sārat, meaning: it moves through the air. Or [the meaning is]: it is taken away, by making it scattered dust (habā'an mabthūthan).

It is also read: "wa-tará al-arḍu" (﴿وَتَرَى الْأَرْضَ﴾) in the passive voice (al-bināʾ lil-mafʿūl), "bārizatan" (﴿بَارِزَةً﴾), meaning there is nothing on it to cover it from what was upon it. "Wa-ḥasharnāhum" (﴿وَحَشَرْنَاهُمْ﴾): and We gathered them, meaning We assembled them at the place of standing (al-mawqif).

It is read: "fa-lam nughādir" (﴿فَلَمْ نُغَادِرْ﴾), with the nūn and with the yā' (﴿يُغَادِرْ﴾). It is said: ghādarahu and aghdarahu, when he left it. From it comes ghadr (ghadr, betrayal), meaning abandoning fidelity. And al-ghadīr (ghadīr, a pool): that which the flood has left behind.

Their condition is likened to the condition of soldiers presented before the ruler, "ṣaffan" (﴿صَفًّا﴾), lined up, visible, so that their group is seen just as each one is seen, with none hiding anyone from another's eyes (lā yuḥjabu aḥadun aḥadan).

"Laqad ji'tumūnā" (﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونَا﴾): that is, We said to them: "You have indeed come to Us." This implied verb is the governing element of the accusative in "yawma nusayyar" (﴿يَوْمَ نُسَيِّرُ﴾). It is also permissible that it be governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember). The meaning is: We have resurrected you just as We originated you, "awwala marratin" (﴿أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ﴾).

It is also said: "you have come to Us barefoot, naked, with nothing with you, just as We created you first," like His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونَا فُرَادَى﴾ ("And you have indeed come to Us alone").

If you ask: why was "ḥasharnāhum" (﴿وَحَشَرْنَاهُمْ﴾) put in the past tense after "nusayyar" and "tará"? I say: to indicate that their gathering was before the moving [of the mountains] and before the appearance [of the earth], so that they witness those great terrors, as if it were said: "We had gathered them before that."

﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (a appointed time): for the fulfillment of what you were promised through the tongues of the prophets, of resurrection and rising.

Their condition is likened to the condition of soldiers presented before the ruler, "ṣaffan" (﴿صَفًّا﴾), lined up, visible, so that their group is seen just as each one is seen, with none hiding anyone from another's eyes (lā yuḥjabu aḥadun aḥadan).

"Laqad ji'tumūnā" (﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونَا﴾): that is, We said to them: "You have indeed come to Us." This implied verb is the governing element of the accusative in "yawma nusayyar" (﴿يَوْمَ نُسَيِّرُ﴾). It is also permissible that it be governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember). The meaning is: We have resurrected you just as We originated you, "awwala marratin" (﴿أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ﴾).

It is also said: "you have come to Us barefoot, naked, with nothing with you, just as We created you first," like His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونَا فُرَادَى﴾ ("And you have indeed come to Us alone").

If you ask: why was "ḥasharnāhum" (﴿وَحَشَرْنَاهُمْ﴾) put in the past tense after "nusayyar" and "tará"? I say: to indicate that their gathering was before the moving [of the mountains] and before the appearance [of the earth], so that they witness those great terrors, as if it were said: "We had gathered them before that."

﴿مَوْعِدًا﴾ (a appointed time): for the fulfillment of what you were promised through the tongues of the prophets, of resurrection and rising.

The Book (al-Kitab) is for the category (li-l-jins), and it is the book of deeds (suhuf al-a'mal). "Woe to us!" they will cry out (ya waylatana, yunadunna), their ruin (halakatahum) which they brought upon themselves, specifically among the ruins. "Neither leaves out a small thing nor a great one" (la yughadiru saghiratan wa la kabiratan): a small thing, and not a great one. This is an expression of comprehensiveness, meaning that it leaves out none of the sins without counting it. That is, it has counted them all, just as you say: "He did not give me a little nor a lot," because things are either small or great. It is also permissible for the meaning to be: "and whether they had minor sins and major sins." It has been said: they did not avoid the major sins, so the minor sins were recorded against them, and these are the scrutinizing (al-munaqashah). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: the small thing is smiling, and the great thing is laughing aloud. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the small thing is touching (al-mAsis), and the great thing is fornication (al-zina).

It is related from al-Fudayl that when he recited it he would say: "By God, cry out over the minor sins before the major sins!"

"Except that it has counted them" (illa ahsaha): except that it has recorded and contained them. "And they will find what they did present in the records" (wa wajadu ma 'amilu hadiran fi al-suhuf), ready. Or it means the recompense for what they did. "And your Lord does not wrong anyone" (wa la yazlimu rabbuka ahadan), so that He writes against someone what he did not do, or increases the punishment of one who deserves it, or punishes him without wrongdoing, as one who attributes injustice to God claims in the punishment of the children of polytheists for the sins of their fathers. [[The phrase "as one who attributes injustice to God claims" is perhaps with the shaddah, i.e., he attributed injustice to Him. (Editor)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 50–51:

Kāna min al-jinn (he was of the jinn) is a resumed statement (kalām mustaʾnaf). [Mahmud said: "His saying, Exalted is He, 'kāna min al-jinn' is a justification for his wickedness... etc." Ahmad said: The truth is with him in this matter, except that his saying "Allah Exalted intended it (taʿammadahu Allāh)" is a phrase that is neither pleasing nor fitting, for deliberate intent (taʿammud) in common usage is attributed to one who sometimes errs and sometimes acts deliberately, so avoiding it with regard to Allah Exalted is obligatory. And Allah is the Granter of success.]

It functions as a restriction (taqlīl) following the exception of Iblis from those who prostrated, as if someone had said: "What was wrong with him that he did not prostrate?" It was said: "He was of the jinn, so he defied (fa-fasaqa) the command of his Lord." The fa here is also for causation (li-l-tasabbub): it makes his being of the jinn the cause of his defiance. For had he been an angel, like all who prostrated to Adam, he would not have defied the command of Allah, because the angels are absolutely protected from sin (maʿṣūmūn al-battah); what is permissible for the jinn and humans is not permissible for them, as He said: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾. This intervening statement is a deliberate act by Allah Exalted to safeguard the angels from any suspicion regarding their infallibility. How far apart is what Allah intended from the claim of one who opposed Him and asserted that he was an angel and a chief over the angels, who disobeyed, was cursed, and was transformed into a devil; then he attributed this (ṣayyar?) to Ibn ʿAbbas. [The phrase "thumma warrakahu" means he attributed it to him (ʿ).]

The meaning of fa-fasaqa ʿan amri rabbihi is: he went out from what his Lord commanded him, namely prostration. He said:

fawāsiqan ʿan qaṣdihā jawāʾiran [The explanation of this witness has passed in the first volume, page 119, so refer to it if you wish. — its corrector.]

Or: he became a defiant disbeliever, by reason of his Lord's command, which is His saying: ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾.

Afa-tattakhidūnahu (Will you then take him): the hamza is for denial and wonder, as if it were said: "After what he has done, do you take him and his offspring as protectors (awliyāʾ) apart from Me, and substitute them for Me? Evil is the substitute for those who choose Iblis instead of Allah, so that obeying him replaces obedience to Him."

Mā ashhadtuhum (I did not make them witnesses): it is also read mā ashhadnāhum (we did not make them witness). The meaning is: you took them as partners to Me in worship, and they would only be partners in it if they were partners in divinity. So He negated their partnership in divinity by saying: ﴿I did not make them witness to the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, that I might rely on them in creating them (li-aʿtaḍida bihim fī khalqihā, i.e., that I might seek their help), ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, i.e., nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others, like His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾.

Wa-mā kuntu muttakhidh al-muḍillīn (And I was not one who takes the misleaders): meaning, and I was not one who would take them as ʿaḍudan, i.e., helpers. The phrase "al-muḍillīn" is placed in the position of the pronoun, as a censure of them for misleading. Since they were not supporters to Me in creation, how can you take them as partners to Me in worship?

It is also read wa-mā kunta (with a fatḥa), addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is: it was not proper for you to rely on them, nor fitting for you to take pride in them. ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) read: wa-mā kunta muttakhidhan al-muḍillīn, with tanwīn, in accordance with the original form. al-Ḥasan read ʿaḍdan with a sukūn on the ḍād and transferred its ḍamma to the ʿayn. It is also read ʿaḍadan with a fatḥa and a sukūn on the ḍād, and ʿuḍdan with two ḍammas, and ʿaḍadan with two fatḥas: these are plurals of ʿāḍid, like khādim and khadam, and rāṣid and raṣad, from ʿaḍadahu, when he strengthened him and helped him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 52–53:

He says, with the ya' and with the nun (i.e., yaqūlu and naqūlu are both read). The attribution of the "partners" to Him, according to their claim, is for the purpose of rebuking them; and He meant the jinn.

Al-mawbiq: the destroyer, from waqaba yaqibu wabūqan, and waqiba yawqibu waqaban, meaning: he perished. And awbaqahu, meaning another caused him to perish. It is permissible for it to be a verbal noun (maṣdar), like al-mawrid and al-maw'id. The meaning: "And We placed between them a valley from the valleys of Hell, a place of destruction and severe punishment, shared, in which they will all perish together." It is related from al-Hasan that mawbiqan means enmity, and the meaning is: an enmity which in its intensity is a destruction, like his saying: "Let not your love be excessive, nor your hatred ruinous." Al-Farra' said: al-bayn means the connection, i.e.: "And We made their association in the world a destruction on the Day of Resurrection."

It is permissible that it refers to the angels, 'Uzayr, 'Isa and Maryam. By al-mawbiq is meant a distant barrier (al-barzakh al-ba'id), i.e.: "And We placed between them a great distance in which the ways are lost because of its extreme remoteness, since they are at the bottom of Hell while they are in the highest of the Gardens."

{fa-ẓannū fa-ayqanū muwāqi'ūhā}: they thought and were certain; muwāqi'ūhā: those who mix with it, those who fall into it. Maṣrifan: a place of escape (mu'addal).

He said:

Zuhayr, "Is there any escape from grey hair?" [[Zuhayr, is there any escape from grey hair ... or is there no immortality for the generous one who spends beyond his means?]]

This is by Abu Kabir al-Hudhali. The hamza is for the vocative. "Zuhayr" is a diminutive (tarkhīm) of Zuhayra, a woman's name. The interrogative is one of denial, meaning: there is no turning away from grey hair, nor any refuge or escape from it. "Am" serves as a transitional disruption (al-idrab al-intiqali) and an interrogative of denial, meaning: rather, the immortality of the generous man who gives freely of what he has, and who exerts himself beyond his capacity in hospitality to guests, is not negated, because generosity does not prevent immortality. It is as if she had been blaming him for his generosity along with the greying and the wounding, so he answered her with that. And in it is an indication of the utmost generosity.

It is as if she had been blaming him for his generosity along with the greying and the wounding, so he answered her with that. And in it is an indication of the utmost generosity.

Most contentious of things (Akthara shay'in jadalan): the most of the things from which contention can arise, if you enumerate them one by one, [are] quarrelsiveness and disputation in falsehood. The accusative of jadalan is a tamyiz (specification), meaning: the contentiousness of man exceeds the contentiousness of everything else. Similar to it is ﴿then behold, he is an open adversary﴾.

The first أَنْ is in the accusative (naṣb), and the second is in the nominative (rafʿ). Before them there is an omitted genitive-construction (muḍāf maḥdhūf), and its intended sense is: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing and asking forgiveness except waiting for the way of the earlier peoples to come upon them﴾, which is the destruction, ﴿or waiting for the punishment to come to them﴾, meaning the punishment of the Hereafter, ﴿face to face (qubulan)﴾, meaning openly before their eyes.

It is read qubulan (as) anwāʿan (kinds). [[His statement "qubulan ʿayānan (face to face). It is read qubulan (as) anwāʿan (kinds)": this reading is with a kasra then a fatḥa. The second is with two ḍammas, as the Ṣiḥāḥ indicates. (ʿ)]] It is the plural of qabīl. And qabulan with two fatḥas means "in front of" (mustaqbalan).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 56:

*Li-yudhiḍū* (لِيُدْحِضُوا): to eliminate and nullify, from *idhḥāḍ al-qadam* (إدحاض القدم), which is the slipping of the foot and its removal from its place of standing.

*Wa-mā undhirū* (وَما أُنْذِرُوا): it is permissible for *mā* to be a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*), in which case the returning pronoun in the relative clause is omitted, meaning: "and that with which they were warned, of the punishment." Or it may be a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*), meaning: "and their warning."

It has been read as *huzuʾan* (هزأ) with a sukūn, meaning: they took them as objects of mockery.

*Wa-jidāluhum* (وجدالهم): their disputation with the Messengers, such as their saying: ﴿You are only human beings like us, and if God had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, and what is similar to that.

Of His signs (bi-ayati rabbihi): that is, of the Qur'an. For this reason the pronoun returned to it in the masculine in His words "that they should understand it" (an yafqahuhu).

But he turned away from them (fa-a'rada 'anha), so he did not take heed when reminded, and did not reflect, and forgot the outcome of what his hands had put forward (wa-nasiya 'aqibata ma qaddamat yadahu), namely disbelief and sins, not pondering over them, nor considering that the evildoer and the doer of good must each have a recompense.

Then he gave the reason for their turning away and forgetting: that they have a seal set upon their hearts (innahum matbu'un 'ala qulubihim). He used the plural after the singular, taking the word "man" (who) according to its form and then according to its meaning. "So they will never be guided" (fa-lan yahtadu): there will never be any guidance from them at all, as if it were impossible for them because of the intensity of their obstinacy, "ever" (abadan), for the entire period of their obligation (mudda al-taklif kulliha).

"Then" (idhan) is a conditional response and an answer. It indicates the negation of their being guided by the Messenger's call, in the sense that they made what should have been the cause of guidance's existence into a cause of its absence. It also indicates that it is an answer from the Messenger, given as if he had said: "What is wrong with me that I do not call them, out of eagerness for their Islam?" Then it was said: "And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided."

The Most Forgiving, the one of perfect forgiveness, the Possessor of mercy, the one described with mercy. Then he cited as evidence for that the fact that He did not hasten to punish the people of Makkah without granting them respite, despite their excessive enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Nay, they have an appointed time, and they shall never find any refuge besides it﴾: the appointed time is the Day of Badr, and "maw'il" means a place of deliverance or a refuge. It is said: "wa'ala" when one is saved, and "wa'ala ilayhi" when one takes refuge in it.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 59:**

﴿And those towns﴾ — he means the towns of the earlier peoples, Thamud, the people of Lot, and others. He pointed to them so that they might take warning.

*Tilka* (تِلْكَ) is the subject (mubtada'), *al-qura* (الْقُرى) is a qualifier (sifah), because demonstrative nouns are qualified by generic nouns, and *ahlaknahum* (أَهْلَكْناهُمْ) is the predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for *tilka al-qura* to be in the accusative, governed by an implied *ahlaknā* (أهلكنا) under the condition of exegetical explanation (shart al-tafsir). The meaning is:

*And those are the people of the towns; We destroyed them when they did wrong, like the wrong of the people of Makkah, and We appointed for their destruction a fixed time*, and We set a known time for their destruction, from which they would not be delayed, just as We set a time for the people of Makkah on the day of Badr. *Al-mahlik* (المهلك) means the act of destruction and its time. It has been recited as *limahlikihim* (لِمَهْلِكِهِمْ) with a fatha on the *mim*, and the *lam* either fatha or kasra, meaning: for their destruction, or the time of their destruction. *Al-mawid* (الموعد) means a time, or a verbal noun.

**Al-Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf*, commentary on Surah 18, verses 60–65**

﴿لِفَتَاهُ﴾ means "to his servant." In a hadith (a report of the Prophet's sayings and actions), the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my female slave,' but let him say 'my young man' (fatāy) and 'my young woman' (fatātī)." It is agreed upon (in al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, and the fuller version is in those collections.

It was said that he was Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun). He was called "his young man" (fatāhu) because he served Musa and followed him. It was also said that he used to take knowledge from him.

If you ask: "﴿لَا أَبْرَحُ﴾ ('I will not cease'), if it means 'I will not depart' (from barahal-makan, to leave the place), then it indicates staying put, not travelling; and if it means 'I will not cease' (lā azāl), then it requires a predicate." I answer: it means "I will not cease," and the predicate has been omitted, because both the circumstance and the statement itself indicate it. As for the circumstance, it was a journey. As for the statement, His words ﴿حَتَّىٰ أَبْلُغَ مَجْمَعَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ﴾ ("until I reach the confluence of the two seas") set a fixed limit which calls for what it is a limit of. So the meaning must be: "I will not cease travelling until I reach the confluence of the two seas."

There is another way of understanding it: the meaning is "my journey will not cease until I arrive," with ﴿حَتَّىٰ أَبْلُغَ﴾ itself being the predicate. When the genitive-modified noun (al-muḍāf) was dropped, the noun that it modified (al-muḍāf ilayhi) was put in its place, which is the first-person pronoun. So the verb shifted from the third-person form to the first-person form. This is a subtle point.

It is also permissible that the meaning be: "I will not cease what I am doing," i.e., "I will persist in travelling and seeking, and will not leave it or abandon it until I arrive," just as you say "I will not leave this place."

**Majma' al-Bahrayn** (the confluence of the two seas) is the place where Musa was promised a meeting with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. It is the meeting point of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea, on the eastern side. It was also said to be Tangier, and it was also said to be Ifriqiya (North Africa). Among the strange interpretations is the claim that "the two seas" are Musa and al-Khidr, because they were two seas of knowledge.

It is read as **majma'** with a kasra on the mim (majma'i), and that form, being irregular, follows the pattern of yaf'il, as in al-mashriq and al-maṭli' (the place of sunrise and sunset). ﴿أَوْ أَمْضِيَ حُقُبًا﴾ ("or I will journey for a long time") means "or I will walk for a long period of time." A ḥuqb is eighty years.

It is related that when Musa prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel, and they settled there after the destruction of the Copts, Allah commanded him to remind his people of the blessing. He stood among them to deliver a sermon, and he mentioned the blessing of Allah and said: "He chose your Prophet and spoke to him directly." They said to him: "We know this. So who among the people is most knowledgeable?" He said: "I am." Allah rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge back to Allah. So He revealed to him: "Rather, a servant of Mine at the confluence of the two seas is more knowledgeable than you, and he is al-Khidr." Al-Khidr lived in the days of Afridun, before Musa, peace be upon him. He was in the vanguard of Dhul-Qarnayn the Great, and he survived until the days of Musa.

It was also said that Musa asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." Al-Khidr lived in the days of Afridun, before Musa, peace be upon him. He was in the vanguard of Dhul-Qarnayn the Great, and he survived until the days of Musa.

It was also said that Musa asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just in judgment?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow his desires." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people to add to his own knowledge, in hope that he might hear a word that guides him to right guidance or turns him away from ruin." He said: "If there is among Your servants someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable of you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where should I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, beside the rock." He said: "O Lord, how can I find him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket, and wherever you lose it, he is there." So he said to his young man: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set off walking, and Musa fell asleep. The fish moved, fell into the sea, and [slipped away]. When the time for the midday meal came, Musa asked for the fish, and his young man informed him that it had fallen into the sea. They came to the rock and found a man covered with his garment. Musa greeted him with peace, and he said: "How is there peace in our land?" Then he identified himself. He said: "O Musa, I have a knowledge that Allah taught me which you do not know, and you have a knowledge that Allah taught you which I do not know."

**Majma' al-Bahrayn** (the confluence of the two seas) is the place where Musa was promised a meeting with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. It is the meeting point of the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea, on the eastern side. It was also said to be Tangier, and it was also said to be Ifriqiya (North Africa). Among the strange interpretations is the claim that "the two seas" are Musa and al-Khidr, because they were two seas of knowledge.

It is read as **majma'** with a kasra on the mim (majma'i), and that form, being irregular, follows the pattern of yaf'il, as in al-mashriq and al-maṭli' (the place of sunrise and sunset). ﴿أَوْ أَمْضِيَ حُقُبًا﴾ ("or I will journey for a long time") means "or I will walk for a long period of time." A ḥuqb is eighty years.

It is related that when Musa prevailed over Egypt with the Children of Israel, and they settled there after the destruction of the Copts, Allah commanded him to remind his people of the blessing. He stood among them to deliver a sermon, and he mentioned the blessing of Allah and said: "He chose your Prophet and spoke to him directly." They said to him: "We know this. So who among the people is most knowledgeable?" He said: "I am." Allah rebuked him because he did not refer knowledge back to Allah. So He revealed to him: "Rather, a servant of Mine at the confluence of the two seas is more knowledgeable than you, and he is al-Khidr." Al-Khidr lived in the days of Afridun, before Musa, peace be upon him. He was in the vanguard of Dhul-Qarnayn the Great, and he survived until the days of Musa.

It was also said that Musa asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just in judgment?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow his desires." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people to add to his own knowledge, in hope that he might hear a word that guides him to right guidance or turns him away from ruin." He said: "If there is among Your servants someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable of you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where should I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, beside the rock." He said: "O Lord, how can I find him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket, and wherever you lose it, he is there." So he said to his young man: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set off walking, and Musa fell asleep. The fish moved, fell into the sea, and [slipped away]. When the time for the midday meal came, Musa asked for the fish, and his young man informed him that it had fallen into the sea. They came to the rock and found a man covered with his garment. Musa greeted him with peace, and he said: "How is there peace in our land?" Then he identified himself. He said: "O Musa, I have a knowledge that Allah taught me which you do not know, and you have a knowledge that Allah taught you which I do not know."

When they boarded the ship, a sparrow came and landed on its edge and pecked at the water. Al-Khidr said: "My knowledge and yours do not diminish the knowledge of Allah by any more than what this sparrow has taken from the sea." ﴿نَسِيَا حُوتَهُمَا﴾ ("they forgot their fish") means they forgot to check on its condition and what would happen with it, which was meant to be a sign of success in the quest.

It was also said: Yusha' forgot to bring the fish forward, and Musa forgot to instruct him about anything concerning it. It was also said that the fish was a salted fish. It was also said that Yusha' carried the fish and the bread in the basket, and they stopped for the night by the shore of a spring called the Spring of Life. Musa fell asleep. When the water's coolness reached the fish, it came back to life. It is related that they both ate from it. It was also said that Yusha' performed ablution from that spring, and water splashed onto the fish, so it came back to life and fell into the water ﴿سَرَبًا﴾ ("making its way into the sea"). Allah stopped the flow of the water over the fish, so that it became like an arch, and it passed through the water like a tunnel.¹ That was a miracle for Musa or for al-Khidr.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاوَزَا﴾ ("when they had passed beyond") the appointed place, which was the rock, because Musa forgot to check on the fish and what had happened to it. And Yusha' forgot to tell Musa what he had seen of the fish coming back to life and falling into the sea.

It was also said: after passing the rock, they travelled through the night and the next day until noon. Fatigue and hunger overcame Musa when they had passed the appointed place; he had not felt tired or hungry before that. So he remembered the fish and asked about it. His words ﴿مِنْ سَفَرِنَا هَذَا﴾ ("from this journey of ours") refer to their travel beyond the rock.

If you ask: how could Yusha' forget that, when someone like him would not forget it? Why did it being a sign of their success in the quest and the fact that it was two miracles—the revival of the salted fish that was eaten from, the spring of water rising like an arch, and its passage through the water like a tunnel—not prevent him from forgetting? And how did the forgetting persist, until they passed the appointed place, travelled a night's journey until midday the next day, and until Musa asked about the fish?

I answer: Satan preoccupied him with his whisperings and took his thoughts in every direction, until forgetfulness overcame him. In addition, he had grown accustomed to seeing such wonders from Musa, peace be upon him, and they were at ease with their companions, so familiarity contributed to his lack of attention.

﴿أَرَأَيْتَ﴾ ("Did you see?") means "tell me."

If you ask: what is the connection of this speech? Each of ﴿أَرَأَيْتَ﴾, ﴿إِذْ أَوَيْنَا﴾ ("when we took refuge"), and ﴿فَإِنِّي نَسِيتُ الْحُوتَ﴾ ("indeed I forgot the fish") seems to have no link to the others?

I answer: When Musa asked for the fish, Yusha' recalled what he had seen of it and his own forgetfulness up to that point. He was overwhelmed and began asking Musa about the reason for it, as if he were saying: "Did you see what befell me when we took refuge at the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish." The rest is omitted.

It was also said: the rock is the one below the River of Oil.

﴿أَنْ أَذْكُرَهُ﴾ ("to remember it") is a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿أَنْسَانِيهُ﴾ ("made me forget it"); meaning: "and nothing made me forget to mention it except Satan."

In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is ﴿أَنْ أَذْكُرَكَهُ﴾ ("to mention it to you").

﴿عَجَبًا﴾ ("in a marvellous way") is the second object of ﴿اتَّخَذَ﴾ ("he took"), like ﴿سَرَبًا﴾; meaning: "and he took its way as a marvellous way," namely that it was like a tunnel. Or it means: "marvellously," at the end of his speech, expressing amazement at his own condition in seeing that wonder and forgetting it, or at what he had seen of the two miracles.

﴿وَمَا أَنْسَانِيهُ إِلَّا الشَّيْطَانُ أَنْ أَذْكُرَهُ﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

It was also said: ﴿عَجَبًا﴾ is a report of Musa's own amazement, peace be upon him. This is not quite right.

﴿ذَٰلِكَ﴾ ("that") refers to taking its way, i.e., "that which we were seeking," because it is the sign of success in the quest, namely meeting al-Khidr, peace be upon him.

It is read as **nabghi** without the yā' when pausing (or joined) and the yā' is better; this is the reading of Abu 'Amr. When stopping, most readers omit the yā', following the script of the Mushaf.

﴿فَارْتَدَّا﴾ ("so they both returned") means they went back on their tracks (adrāj), i.e., they retraced their steps on the path by which they had come.² ﴿قَصَصًا﴾ ("retracing") means they went back tracing their steps, that is, they followed their traces closely. Or ﴿فَارْتَدَّا﴾ means they returned following exactly the way they had come.

﴿رَحْمَةً مِنْ عِنْدِنَا﴾ ("a mercy from Us") is revelation and prophethood. ﴿مِنْ لَدُنَّا﴾ ("from Our presence") means what is specially Ours of knowledge, which is informing about the unseen.

---

¹ The phrase "in a tunnel-like manner" translates the author's note: in *al-Sihah*, "al-sarab" is a hole in the ground. One says: "The wild animal went into its burrow," and "the fox slipped into its den." (Mu'jam note.)

² The author's note: "al-darj" is the path, and its plural is "al-adraj." From this comes the phrase "I returned along my adraj," meaning I returned along the road by which I had come, as in *al-Sihah*.

rushdan: it is read with two fatha vowels, and also with a damma and a sukun. That is, "knowledge that has rectitude," (meaning) that I may be guided by it in my religion. If you say: Does his need to learn from another in his time not indicate that he (i.e., the other) was, as it has been said, Musa ibn Maysha, not Musa ibn Imran, since the Prophet must be the most knowledgeable people of his time and their imam, the one referred to in matters of religion?

I say: There is no disgrace for the Prophet in taking knowledge from a prophet like himself; what would be disgraceful is for him to take it from one who is inferior to him. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of the wife of Ka'b, claims that al-Khidr is not the companion of Musa, and that Musa is Musa ibn Maysha." He said: "The enemy of Allah has lied." [[Ibn Ishaq related it in al-Maghazi from al-Hasan ibn 'Umara from al-Hakam from Sa'id ibn Jubayr with this wording. The whole story is related in the two Sahihs with a different wording, from the narration of 'Amr ibn Dinar from Sa'id.]]

He denied the ability to be patient with him, using emphatic phrasing. [[Mahmud said: "He denied the ability in emphatic form... etc." Ahmad said: What shows that Musa, peace be upon him, was driven to rush into denunciation only by fervour and zeal for the truth is that when he tore the ship he said: "Have you torn it to drown its people?" and did not say "to drown us." He forgot himself and occupied himself with others, in the very state in which every person says "myself, myself," not turning back for wealth or children, and that is the state of drowning. Glory be to Him who made His prophets and chosen ones patient in advising creation, compassionate toward them and tender with them, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them all.]] It seems as if this is not valid or correct. He gave as the reason that he undertakes matters which, outwardly, are objectionable. A righteous man, let alone a prophet, cannot restrain himself from recoiling, being displeased and distressed when he sees such things, and he begins to denounce them. "Khubran" is a tamyiz (accusative of specification), meaning: "his knowledge did not encompass it," in the sense of "you did not inform him," so its being in the accusative is that of a masdar (verbal noun).

It seems the passage contains an error in its first line: "أولا في محل" is a garbled fragment, but I'll translate the text as given.

"And I will not disobey" is in the accusative position, conjoined to "patient" (ṣābiran), meaning: "You will find me patient and not disobedient."

"Not" in its position is conjoined to "you will find me" (sa-tajidunī). Mūsā (peace be upon him), out of his eagerness for knowledge and its increase, hoped that he could be patient with him even after al-Khiḍr had made clear the reality of the matter. So he promised patience, making it conditional on God's will, knowing the severity and difficulty of the matter, and that the zeal that seizes the reformer when he sees corruption is something unbearable. This is in addition to his knowledge that the infallible prophet, whom God commanded him to travel to, follow, and acquire knowledge from, is free from engaging in anything that would be a blemish in religion, and that what appears outwardly to be disagreeable must have an inner goodness and beauty. How much more so when one does not know it.

Some read it as "fa-la tas'alnnī" with the heavy nūn (nūn al-tawkīd al-thaqīla). The meaning is: among the conditions of following me is that when you see something from me, and you know it to be correct but its right aspect is hidden from you, so that you become angry (ḥamiyta; in the Ṣiḥāḥ, ḥamiyta ʿalayhi, with kasra, means "I became angry") and it troubles you inwardly, you must not open a question to me about it or argue with me over it, until I am the one who opens it to you. This is among the manners of the student with the scholar, and of the one who is followed with the follower.

So they set out along the seashore seeking a boat. When they boarded, its people said: "These two are thieves," and ordered them out. The owner of the boat said: "I see the faces of prophets." It is also said: they recognised al-Khidr, so they carried them without a fare. When they reached the deep water, al-Khidr took the axe and damaged the boat by prying up two of its planks on the side facing the water. Then Musa began to stop up the breach with his garments, and said: ﴿Have you damaged it in order to drown its people?﴾ It is also read: "to drown" (litughharriqa), with the doubled letter, and "and drown its people" (wa-liyughriqa ahlaha), where "its people" is in the nominative case as the subject.

﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾: you have done a great matter. From amira al-amr, meaning it became great. The poet said:

"Indeed the peoples have met from me a calamity (nukr),
a grave, mighty, dreadful misfortune (dahiya dahyaa idda imra)."

Al-nukr: the reprehensible thing. Al-dahiya: an unpleasant event among the hardships of time. Al-dahyaa: an intensification of its severity. Al-idd: the utterly reprehensible. Al-imr: a great thing. It is said: amira al-shay' (with kasra): it became great. He describes himself as inflicting severe harm on the enemies.

It is permissible that the speech is of the type of tajrid (abstraction, where a speaker addresses himself as another).

With what I forgot (bi-ma nasītu): by "that which I forgot" (bi-alladhi nasītuhu), or "something I forgot" (bi-shay'in nasītuhu), or "my forgetting" (bi-nisyānī). He meant that he forgot his covenant, and there is no blame upon one who forgets.

Or the speech was put in the form of a prohibition against holding him to account for forgetting, giving the impression that he had forgotten, so as to extend his excuse for the objection. This is among the indirect expressions (ma'ārīḍ al-kalām) by which one avoids lying while still reaching the aim, like the saying of Abraham: ﴿This is my sister﴾ and ﴿I am sick﴾.

Or by "forgetting" he meant "leaving" (al-tark), that is: do not hold me to account for what I left of your instruction the first time. It is said: rahiqahu, when it overtook him, and arhaqahu iyyāhu, meaning: do not overwhelm me with hardship (ʿusran) in my affair, which is his following him; that is, do not make my following you difficult for me, and make it easy for me by overlooking and by not pressing me with questions. It was also read ʿusran with two dammas (ʿusurran? no: ʿusran, with two ḍammas: ʿusuran).

So he killed him ﴿فَقَتَلَهُ﴾. It was said: his killing was by cutting his neck. It was said: he struck his head against the wall. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: he laid him down and then slaughtered him with a knife.

If you ask: why is it said ﴿حَتَّى إِذا رَكِبا فِي السَّفِينَةِ خَرَقَها﴾ ("until, when they boarded the ship, he tore it") without a fa' (the particle "then"), but ﴿حَتَّى إِذا لَقِيا غُلاماً فَقَتَلَهُ﴾ ("until, when they met a boy, he killed him") with one? I say: he made his tearing of the ship the response (jaza', "apodosis") to the conditional clause (shart, "protasis"), and made his killing a part of the conditional clause, conjoined to it. The response is his saying: ﴿أَقَتَلْتَ﴾ ("Did you kill...?"). If you ask: why were the two treated differently? I say: because the tearing of the ship did not immediately follow the boarding, whereas the killing did immediately follow the meeting with the boy.

It was read as ﴿زاكية﴾ (zakiyya) and ﴿زكية﴾ (zakiyya, with a different vowelling), and it means pure of sins. This is either because it was pure in his view, since he had not seen it commit a sin, or because it was a child who had not reached the age of puberty (al-hunth, "the age of legal responsibility"). ﴿بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ﴾ ("without a soul") means that it had not killed a soul, so that retaliation could be exacted from it.

From Ibn Abbas: Najdah al-Haruri wrote to him: "How was his killing permitted, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade the killing of children?" He wrote back: "If you know of the condition of children what the knower of Moses knew, then it is permitted for you to kill them." [Abu Ya'la transmitted something similar and said at its end, "and that was permitted for you," and in another narration of his, "I said: but you do not know," so avoid them. Its origin is in Muslim, though in a different context. Its beginning: Najdah ibn 'Amir wrote to Ibn Abbas asking him about the killing of children... the hadith. In it: "You asked me about the killing of children. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not kill them except when he knew of them what the companion of Moses knew of the boy he killed."]

﴿نُكْراً﴾ (nukran, "a reprehensible thing"). It is read with two dammas (nukr), and it means the reprehensible. It was said that nukr is less than imr (a grave matter), because killing one soul is easier than drowning the people of the ship. It was also said: its meaning is that you have done something more reprehensible than the first, because that was a tear that could be repaired by patching, whereas this has no way of being repaired.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the addition ﴿لَكَ﴾ ("for you")? I say: it is the emphasis of confronting him with reproach for breaking the stipulation, and the branding of him with lack of patience at the second time.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 76:

"Then if I ask you about anything after this (ba'dahā), then do not keep company with me (falā tuṣāḥibnī)." That is: after this turn or this question. "Do not keep company with me" means do not come near me, and if you seek my companionship, do not follow me in that.

It was also read as "falā tuṣḥibnī," meaning "do not be my companion" (falā takun ṣāḥibī). It was also read as "falā tuṣaḥibnī," meaning: do not make me accompany you, and do not make me your companion. "Min ladunnī ʿudhran" means: "you have indeed given me an excuse (qad aʿdhartu)." It was also read "ladunī" with the nun lightened, and "ladunī" with the dal sukun and the nun kasra, like their saying "ʿaḍd" for "ʿaḍud" (ʿaḍud, meaning "arm").

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

"May Allah have mercy on my brother Musa; he was modest, so he said that (istaḥyā fa-qāla dhālika), and said: 'May Allah have mercy upon us and upon my brother Musa. Had he remained with his companion, he would have seen the most wondrous of wonders.'" [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh through the narration of Dawud ibn Abi Hind from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmayr from Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, relating the story. In it: "May Allah have mercy upon us and upon Musa. He was modest at that point, and said: 'If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep company with me'—the verse.".]] Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban, through the narration of Hamza al-Zayyat, from Abu Ishaq, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from Ubayy, in the course of a longer hadith. Its original source is in Muslim.

The people of a town: it is Antioch. It was also said: al-Ubulla, which is the farthest land of God from heaven. **That they should host them.** It is also read *yudayyifuhumā*. It is said *ḍāfahu* when he became his guest (*ḍayf*). Its literal sense is "he inclined toward him," from "the arrow deviated from the target." Its counterpart is *zārahu* ("he visited him"), from *izwirār* ("turning aside"). *Aḍāfahu* and *ḍayyafahu* mean "he lodged him and made him his guest."

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "They were a town of miserable people" [[Recorded by al-Nasā'ī, through the narration of Isrā'īl from Ibn Isḥāq, from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbās, from Ubayy, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying, "they refused to host them." He said: "They were a town of miserable people." It is also in Muslim with the wording: "So they both set out until, when they came to the people of a miserable town."]]. It was also said: the worst towns are those in which the guest is not hosted and the wayfarer's right is not recognized.

**Wants to collapse:** the will (*irāda*) is borrowed for approaching and being on the verge, just as concern (*hamm*) and resolve (*ʿazm*) are borrowed for that. The poet said:

*In a desert where their heads trembled, trembling like axes when they wanted to be fitted with blades.* [[By al-Rā'ī, describing camels in a desert (*mahmah*), i.e., a wasteland. *Qalaqat*: moved. *Hāmātuhā*: their heads. *Qalaq al-fu's*: like the movement of axes (*fu's*, pl. *fu's*, is the digging tool). *Idhā aradna*: i.e., the axes. *Nuṣūlan*: i.e., came close to it. So "wanted" is a figurative (*majāz mursal*) usage. *Nuṣūl* of the axe is the blade's coming out of its handle. *Nuṣūl* in anything means coming out, and *inṣāl* means bringing out. He likened the heads of the camels with their necks to axes.]]

He also said:

*The spear wants the chest of Abū Barrā', and turns away from the blood of Banū ʿUqayl.* [[The "wanting" here is a figure for "directing oneself toward." It is also permissible that the attribution is figurative, since the one who wants is the owner of the spear. The more correct view is that he likened the spear to a person by implicit metaphor (*makniyya*), and attributing the wanting and the turning away to it is imaginative evocation (*takhyīl*). That is: it wants to drink from the chest of Abū Barrā', not from the blood of these people.]]

Ḥassān said:

*Indeed, a time that wraps my union with Jamal, is a time that intends kindness.* [[By Ḥassān ibn Thābit. *Laffaytu al-shay'*: I folded and rolled up the thing. *Al-shaml*: the scattered; it is also applied to what is gathered of affairs. *Jamal*: the name of his beloved. It is also narrated as "with Saʿdā." He says: the time that gathers my union with my beloved is a time that intends kindness to them, and it wants it. *Hamm* is also of this type of *rad*, meaning: a time that wants kindness, not harm, as is the custom of time. So time is likened to a person who can intend kindness, by implicit metaphor, and *hamm* is imaginative evocation. It is possible that attributing the concern to it is a rational figure (*majāz ʿaqlī*), like attributing the wrapping, and both are in truth to God.]] I have heard someone say: "The lamp resolved to be extinguished" and "it sought to be extinguished." If speech, utterance, complaint, truthfulness, falsehood, silence, rebellion, refusal, pride, obedience, and other such things are borrowed for inanimate and non-rational things, then what about will? He said:

*When the saddle-straps say to the belly-band "Stretch"* [[The explanation of this witness was given earlier, on page 181 of the first volume, so refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector).]]

*they say "Tighten" to the saddle's girth.*

*The lute does not speak until the wood speaks.* [[*Fa-istanṭaqa al-ʿūd qad ṭāla al-sukūt bihi / lā yanṭiqu al-lahwu ḥattā yanṭiqa al-ʿūd*: "He sought the lute to speak, its silence having lasted long; the entertainment does not speak until the lute speaks." By Abū Nuwās. He likened the sound of the lute, in its straightness and beauty, to speech through singing, by explicit metaphor (*taṣrīḥiyya*). Or he likened the lute to a person by implicit metaphor, and "speaking" is imaginative evocation. The *sīn* and *tā'* indicate seeking. Silence is a complement (*tarshīḥ*) of that, since it is the opposite of artificiality. By "the speech of entertainment" is meant its increase and beauty, so it is of the type of *mushākala* (equivalence of expression). Whether it is literal, figurative, metonymic, or a fourth category is a disputed matter among the scholars, explained at length in the science of rhetoric (*bayān*).]]

*And it complained to me with a tear and a neigh.* [[*Fa-zāra min waqʿ al-qanā bi-labānihi / wa-shakā ilayya bi-ʿabratin wa-taḥammuḥi / law kāna yadrī mā al-muḥāwaratu shtakā / wa-lakāna law ʿalima al-kalāma mukallimī*: By ʿAntara ibn Shaddād, from his Muʿallaqa, describing his horse: it turned aside from the impact of the spears on its breast, the *labān* being the place of the breast-strap on its chest. He likened it to a rational being by implicit metaphor, and "complaint" is imaginative evocation. *ʿAbra*: weeping. *Tahammuḥ*: the sound of neighing, resembling longing. If it knew what dialogue and conversation are, it would have complained to me and addressed me literally, but it only complains to me with the tear and the neigh. He explained it with his saying: "and it would have been speaking to me, if it knew speech," and that is hyperbole about the intensity of the war.]]

*So if my suspicion is truthful, and she is truthful about me* [[*Lahfī ʿalā al-qawmi alladhīna tajammaʿū / bi-dhī al-sayyidi lam yalqawhu ʿaliyyan wa-lā ʿamrā / fa-in yaku ẓannī ṣādiqan wa-huwa ṣādiqī / bi-shamlatin yuḥbisuhum bihā maḥbasan waʿran*: By the woman Kanz, mother of Shamla ibn Bard al-Minqarī. *Dhū al-Sayyid* (with a kasra) is the place of the battle. *Al-sayyid*: the wolf. Her saying "wa-huwa ṣādiqī" is a parenthetical clause. *Bi-shamlatin*: is connected to *ẓannī*. She says: "Alas for me over the people who gathered at that place, and whom neither of these two horsemen met, so they killed Bard, Shamla's father. If my suspicion about him is truthful, though his habit is to be truthful with me, Shamla will hold them in that battle in a hard confinement and take revenge for his father." It is also permissible that *maḥbasan* is an adverbial accusative (*ẓarf*) that is substituted for *bihā*. The suspicion is likened to one from whom truthfulness in report is possible, by metonymy (*kināya*), and "truthful" is imaginative evocation for that. Or the meaning is: if my suspicion corresponds to reality.]] And when anger was silenced from Moses.

*A rebellious rock and a white fortress resisted.* [[*Wa-qad qālat al-Zabbā li-ḥiṣni Samawʾal / tamarrada Māriddun wa-ʿazza al-Abqaru*: Al-Zabbā, queen of the Jazīra, said that, to the fortress of Samawʾal. *Māriddun* is the fortress of Dūmat al-Jandal. *Al-Abqar* is the fortress of Samawʾal. She targeted both of them, and they proved difficult for her, so she said this, and it became a proverb. His saying "to the fortress of Samawʾal" means: and to the fortress of Dūmat al-Jandal. *Tamarrada*: became smooth and soft; *marada*, *maradan*, and *marūdatan*, when something is smooth without hair, and a place without vegetation. Or *tamarrada* means "became a devil," and its people acted like the rebellious jinn, so no one can climb it. *ʿAzza*: if its present tense is with a *ḍamma* on the ʿayn, it is transitive, meaning "overcame"; if it is with a *kasra*, it is intransitive, meaning "refused." The meaning is that she could not reach her aim from them, because of their people's bravery.]]

And to some of them:

*His eyelids refuse him sleep, a concern that, when the worries are obeyed, becomes rebellious.*

*The buttocks and the breast refused, in their shirts, to touch the bellies and to touch the backs.* [[*Abat al-rawādifu wa-al-thadyu li-qumṣihā / massa al-buṭūni wa-an tamassa ẓuhūrā / wa-idhā al-riyāḥu maʿa al-ʿashiyyi tanāwaḥat / naynahunna ḥāsidatan wa-hunna ghayūrā*: *Al-ibāʾ* is voluntary refusal. He likened the buttocks and the breast, because of their largeness, to one who can do that, by implicit metaphor, and *ibāʾ* is imaginative evocation. The closer view is that it is a figure of metonymy (*majāz mursal*), and what is meant by it is general prevention. What follows is a metonymy for the fullness of her breasts and the size of her buttocks and the slenderness of her waist. There is an interweaving (*lafф*) and spreading (*nashr*) that is not in order, because touching the bellies relates to the breast, and touching the backs relates to the buttocks. He expressed the plural by the singular figuratively, or he considered the parts, so the figurative usage is in the singular of the plural. *Al-thadī* with a shadda is the plural of *thadī* without shadda. *Al-qumṣ* is the plural of *qamīṣ*. *Tanāwaḥa al-jabalān*: they faced each other. So the meaning of *tanāwuḥ* is facing, such that some winds come from in front and some from behind, so her buttocks and breasts appear, and the garments cling to her waist, so her slenderness is revealed, thus alerting the envious one to her, and the jealous one is stirred because he dislikes that from the winds. *Hāja al-shay'*: it became agitated; *hājahu*: he agitated it; *hayyajahu*: he agitated it. What is here is from the middle. It is also permissible that it is likened by implicit metaphor. Or their soft sounds are likened to tanāwuḥ by explicit metaphor, then that is made a metonymy for their facing each other, because they only have sounds when they face each other and are disturbed. *Maʿa* is in the sense of *fī*.]]

They both said: "We came obedient." [Note: this final section is followed by a passage about a critic misreading the pronoun as referring to al-Khiḍr. Translation continues below.]

Indeed, it has reached me that some of those who distort the words of God Most High, from those who lack knowledge, used to make the pronoun refer to al-Khiḍr, because what was in it of the blight of ignorance and the sickness of understanding, he saw the highest speech at the lowest level, so he carried it to return it to what he holds to be more correct and more eloquent, and he held that what was further from figurative usage was more inclusive of inimitability (*iʿjāz*).

**Yanqaḍḍa** (to collapse): when its falling quickens, from the swooping of a bird, which is *yaf'allu*, the reflexive of *qaḍḍadtuhu*. It was also said: *if'alla* from *al-naqḍ*, like *iḥmarra* from *al-ḥumra*. It is also read *an yanqaḍa* from *al-naqḍ*, and *an yanqāṣa*, from *infāṣat al-sinnu* when it splits lengthwise. Dhū al-Rumma said:

*......... distant and close.*

*It covers the lair with its two horns and destroys it, from the large fallen sand, sloping and ready to fall.* [[By Dhū al-Rumma, describing a wild bull. *Al-kināsu*: the animal's den. *Rawqāhu*: its two horns. *Al-minqāṣ* (like *al-mukhtār*): what falls from the side of the length of the den. *Al-mankathib* (with three letters): what is gathered. It is narrated as *munqāḍ* with a dotted letter. The meaning is one: that is, it digs the den with its horn, so that it is hidden from the rain, and what falls and gathers from the loose, soft sand destroys it.]] With the unpointed *ṣād*.

**So He raised it up.** It was said: he raised it with his hand. It was said: he wiped it with his hand, and it stood up and became straight. It was said: he raised it with a pillar he propped it with. It was said: he tore it down and built it. It was also said that the height of the wall in the sky was a hundred cubits. The situation was one of compulsion and need for food, and the need had gripped them both to the last of a person's earnings, which is begging, but they found no one to comfort them. When he raised the wall, Moses could not contain himself, seeing the deprivation and the touch of need, and said: "**If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it.**" That is, you could have asked a payment for your work, so that we might recover and drive off the necessity with it.

It is read *la-takhadhta* (with the *tā'* of *takhadha*). The *tā'* in *takhadha* is original, as in *tabiʿa*, and *ittakhadha* is its reflexive form (*ifta'ala*) from it, like *ittabaʿa* from *tabiʿa*. It has nothing to do with *al-akhdh* (taking).

Question: To what does this refer? Answer: The parting between the two of them is conceived of as taking place when its appointed time arrives, as Musa (peace be upon him) said: "If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep company with me." So he pointed to it, made it the subject (mubtada') and predicated something of it, just as you say, "This is your brother." Thus "this" does not refer to anything other than the parting. It is also permissible that it refers to the third question, meaning: this objection is the cause of the parting. The original form is: "This is parting between me and you." Ibn Abi 'Ablah also read it this way, so the verbal noun (masdar) is annexed to the adverbial noun of time (zarf), just as it is annexed to the object (maf'ul bihi).

**[For the poor]** It was said that they were ten brothers, five of them disabled and five working at sea. **[Behind them]** means in front of them, as in His saying ﴿and behind them is a barrier﴾. It was also said it means behind them: their route on the way back passed by it, and they did not know what had happened to it. So God informed al-Khidr of it, and the king was **al-Jalandā** [*Note: In al-Khazin, his name was al-Jalandā al-Azdī, and he was a disbeliever. It was also said that his name was Harad ibn Bard. (ʿA)*]. If you say: His saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ is caused by fear of a usurper over it, so its proper place would be after the cause, why did he put it first? I say:

[*Note: Mahmud said: "If you say: His saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ is caused by fear of a usurper over it..." Ahmad said: It seems he took the cause of the damage to be that the ship belonged to the poor, then he explained the connection between this cause and its effect by mentioning the custom of the king in seizing ships. This is the proper order in giving a reason: the ruling is linked to its cause, and then the connection is clarified afterwards. There is no need to make it come first and to intend that it be delayed, and God knows best. I have marvelled greatly at the eloquence of these verses and the variation in their style. Do you not see that in the first he attributed the action to himself alone, saying ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾, and in the second he attributed it to the plural pronoun of majesty, saying ﴿so We wished that their Lord would replace them﴾ and ﴿so We feared that he would burden them﴾? Perhaps attributing the first to himself alone was out of courtesy towards God, since the intent was damage, so he showed courtesy and attributed the damage to himself. As for attributing the second to the plural pronoun, the apparent reason is the manner of the king's close associates saying "We have ordered such-and-such" or "We have arranged such-and-such", when they mean the king's order and arrangement. This is confirmed by His saying in the third ﴿so your Lord wished that they reach their maturity﴾. See how these styles differ, and they did not come in one repeated pattern that the ear tires of and rejects. This variation also contains the observance of the secrets mentioned. Glory be to the Subtle, the All-Aware.*]

The intent of the delay is not what is meant here; it was placed first for emphasis. Also, fear of the usurper is not the cause alone, but together with the fact that it belonged to the poor. So it is like your saying: "Zayd, my opinion is that he is staying."

It was also said that in the recitation (**qira'a**) of Ubayy and Abdullah it reads: **"Every sound ship."**

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verses 80–82:

It is recited by al-Jahdari, with the reading (qira'a) "wa-kāna abawāhu mu'minān" (﴿and his two parents were believers﴾), where "kāna" contains a *ḍamīr al-sha'n* (pronoun of the matter, i.e., the dummy subject). ﴿So we feared that he would overwhelm them with rebellion and disbelief﴾: so we feared that he would cover the two believing parents with his rebellion against them and his ingratitude for their blessings, through his disobedience and bad conduct, and that he would bring upon them evil and affliction. Or his rebellion and disbelief would be joined to their faith, so that two believers and a rebellious disbeliever would be gathered in one house. ﴿He would lead them astray with his own corruption and mislead them with his error﴾, so that they would apostatize because of him, rebel, and disbelieve after faith. Al-Khadir only feared this because God Most High had informed him of the boy's condition and revealed to him the secret of his affair. His command to kill him was like taking him away (ikhtiram) because of a corruption he knew of in his life.

In the recitation of Ubayy: ﴿So your Lord feared﴾. The meaning is: your Lord disliked (it), with the dislike of one who fears the bad outcome of the matter, and so changed it. It is also permissible that His saying ﴿fa-khashīnā (so we feared)﴾ is a quotation of God's words, meaning: so We disliked, like His saying ﴿li-ahaba laki (to bestow upon you)﴾.

It is recited as "yubaddilahumā" with the doubled letter (tashdīd). "Zakāh" means purity and cleanness from sins. "Ruḥm" means mercy and compassion.

It is reported that a girl was born to them and a prophet married her, and she bore a prophet through whom God guided a nation of the nations. It is said that she bore seventy prophets. It is also said that God replaced them with a believing son like them. It is said that the names of the two boys were Asram and Sarim. The boy who was killed was named al-Husayn.

Scholars differed about the treasure (kanz). It is said: it was buried wealth of gold and silver. [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani and Ibn 'Adi through the chain of Makhul, from Umm al-Darda', from Abu al-Darda'; in it is Yazid ibn al-Sana'ani, who is weak.]] It is also said: it was a gold tablet on which was written: "I am amazed at one who believes in destiny, how he grieves; I am amazed at one who believes in provision, how he toils; I am amazed at one who believes in death, how he rejoices; I am amazed at one who believes in reckoning, how he is heedless; I am amazed at one who knows the world and its turning over its people, how he is content with it. There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." [[Narrated by al-Bazzar from the narration of Ibn Hujayra, from Abu Dharr, marfū', with this text and more complete than it. He said: we do not know it from Abu Dharr except through this chain. Al-Daraqutni narrated in Gharā'ib Malik through the chain of Muhammad ibn Salih ibn Fayruz, from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the treasure," and he mentioned it; and he said: this is false from Malik. Ibn 'Adi narrated it, and through the narration of Abyan ibn Sufyan and al-Tabarani in al-Du'a', through the narration of Rushdayn ibn Sa'd, both from Abu Hazim, from Ibn 'Abbas, something similar. And from 'Ali, with a wording like the author's, al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Shu'ab through the narration of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from al-Nazzal ibn Sabra, from him. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from another route, from 'Ali, marfū'. Ibn Shahin narrated it in al-Janā'iz, and al-Wahidi through the narration of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Saddi al-Saghir, from Ayyan, from Anas, also marfū'. Aban and al-Saddi al-Saghir are abandoned narrators.]] It is also said: it was knowledge written in it. The apparent meaning, given its absoluteness, is that it was wealth.

It is reported from Qatada: "The treasure was made lawful for those before us and forbidden to us, and booty was forbidden to them and made lawful for us." He meant His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾. ﴿And their father was righteous﴾: this is a reckoning of the righteousness of their father and a safeguarding of his right concerning them. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq: "Between the two boys and the father in whose merit they were protected there were seven fathers." It is reported from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said to one of the Kharijites in a conversation that took place between them: "By what did Allah protect the two boys?" He said: "By the righteousness of their father." He said: "Then my father and my grandfather are better than him." He said: "Allah has informed us that you are a contentious people."

﴿Mercy﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), or an infinitive in the accusative governed by ﴿your Lord desired﴾, since it has the meaning of ﴿He had mercy on them﴾.

﴿And I did not do it﴾: I did not do what you saw ﴿of my own accord﴾, by my own ijtihad and opinion. Rather, I did it by the command of Allah.
