Scholars differed about the treasure (kanz). It is said: it was buried wealth of gold and silver. [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani and Ibn 'Adi through the chain of Makhul, from Umm al-Darda', from Abu al-Darda'; in it is Yazid ibn al-Sana'ani, who is weak.]] It is also said: it was a gold tablet on which was written: "I am amazed at one who believes in destiny, how he grieves; I am amazed at one who believes in provision, how he toils; I am amazed at one who believes in death, how he rejoices; I am amazed at one who believes in reckoning, how he is heedless; I am amazed at one who knows the world and its turning over its people, how he is content with it. There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." [[Narrated by al-Bazzar from the narration of Ibn Hujayra, from Abu Dharr, marfū', with this text and more complete than it. He said: we do not know it from Abu Dharr except through this chain. Al-Daraqutni narrated in Gharā'ib Malik through the chain of Muhammad ibn Salih ibn Fayruz, from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the treasure," and he mentioned it; and he said: this is false from Malik. Ibn 'Adi narrated it, and through the narration of Abyan ibn Sufyan and al-Tabarani in al-Du'a', through the narration of Rushdayn ibn Sa'd, both from Abu Hazim, from Ibn 'Abbas, something similar. And from 'Ali, with a wording like the author's, al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Shu'ab through the narration of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from al-Nazzal ibn Sabra, from him. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from another route, from 'Ali, marfū'. Ibn Shahin narrated it in al-Janā'iz, and al-Wahidi through the narration of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Saddi al-Saghir, from Ayyan, from Anas, also marfū'. Aban and al-Saddi al-Saghir are abandoned narrators.]] It is also said: it was knowledge written in it. The apparent meaning, given its absoluteness, is that it was wealth.

It is reported from Qatada: "The treasure was made lawful for those before us and forbidden to us, and booty was forbidden to them and made lawful for us." He meant His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾. ﴿And their father was righteous﴾: this is a reckoning of the righteousness of their father and a safeguarding of his right concerning them. It is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq: "Between the two boys and the father in whose merit they were protected there were seven fathers." It is reported from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said to one of the Kharijites in a conversation that took place between them: "By what did Allah protect the two boys?" He said: "By the righteousness of their father." He said: "Then my father and my grandfather are better than him." He said: "Allah has informed us that you are a contentious people."

﴿Mercy﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), or an infinitive in the accusative governed by ﴿your Lord desired﴾, since it has the meaning of ﴿He had mercy on them﴾.

﴿And I did not do it﴾: I did not do what you saw ﴿of my own accord﴾, by my own ijtihad and opinion. Rather, I did it by the command of Allah.

Dhu al-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned One) is Alexander, who ruled the world. It has been said that two believers ruled the earth, Dhu al-Qarnayn and Sulayman, and two disbelievers, Nimrod and Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it through Mujahid. He said: "Only four people ruled the whole earth: two believers and two disbelievers," and then he mentioned it.]], and he came after Nimrod. Scholars differed about him. It was said that he was a righteous servant whom God granted dominion over the earth, gave knowledge and wisdom, clothed in awe, and subjected to him light and darkness, so that when he travelled, light guided him from in front and darkness surrounded him from behind. It was also said that he was a prophet, and it was said that he was an angel.

It is related from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he heard a man say, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" He said, "Lord, forgive us! Are you not content to name yourselves after the prophets, that you must name yourselves after the angels?" It is related from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that the clouds were subjected to him, the means were extended to him, and light was spread for him. When he was asked about him, he said: "God loved him, so he loved him." Ibn al-Kawwa asked him, "What is Dhu al-Qarnayn? Was he a king or a prophet?" He said:

"He was neither a king nor a prophet, but a righteous servant who struck his right horn in the obedience of God and died. Then God raised him up, and he struck his left horn and died. Then God raised him up and named him Dhu al-Qarnayn, and there is one like him among you."

It was said that he used to call them to monotheism (tawhid, affirming the oneness of God), and they would kill him, and God would bring him back to life.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he traversed the two horns of the world [[I have not found it traced to the Prophet ﷺ. It was narrated by al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif, through Abd al-Aziz ibn Imran, from Sulayman ibn Asid, from al-Zuhri, who said: "He was only named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the horn of the sun at its setting and the horn of the sun at its rising."]], meaning its two sides, east and west. It was also said that he had two horns, that is, two braids. It was said that two generations of people passed away in his time. It is related from Wahb that he was called so because he ruled the Romans and the Persians, and it is also reported that he ruled the Romans and the Turks. And from him: the two sides of his head were of copper. It was also said that his crown had two horns, and that on his head was something resembling two horns.

It is possible that he was given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram (kabsh) because he butts his rivals. He was from the Romans, the son of an old woman who had no other child.

The questioners were the Jews, who asked him as a test. It was also said that Abu Jahl and his followers asked him. The address in ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (upon you) is to one of the two groups. ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ (from everything) means from the means of everything, namely the things he desired among his aims and purposes in his kingdom. ﴿سَبَباً﴾ (a means) means a path leading to it. A sabab (means) is that by which one reaches a goal, whether knowledge, power, or equipment. So he desired to reach the west, and ﴿فَأَتْبَعَ سَبَباً﴾ (then he followed a means) that would bring him there, until he arrived. Likewise he desired the east, and he followed a means, and he desired to reach the two barriers, and he followed a means.

It is read ﴿فَأَتْبَعَ﴾ (then he followed) with a different vowelling. It is read ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (muddy), from ḥamiʾat al-bi'r, when the well becomes filled with mud (ḥamʾa). And ﴿حَامِيَةٍ﴾ (hot) means "ḥārra" (burning).

It is related from Abu Dharr: "I was riding behind the Messenger of God ﷺ on a camel, and he saw the sun when it set, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where this sets?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It sets in a hot spring.'"

[[This is so in copies of al-Kashshaf: "on a camel." But in the books of hadith it is "on a donkey," and riding behind is not mentioned. It is related by Abu Dawud and al-Hakim through al-Hakam ibn Utayba, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, from his father, from Abu Dharr, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I was with the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he was on a donkey, and the sun was setting. He said: 'Do you know where this sets?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It sets in a hot spring.'" Al-Hakim added: "not hamzated" [i.e., ḥāmiya without hamza]. It was also narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, and added: "And it goes on until it prostrates before its Lord beneath the Throne. When it is time for it to rise, God permits it, and when God wants to make it rise from its west, He holds it back and says: 'Rise from where you set.' That is the time when faith will not benefit a soul." Al-Hakim said: "Sufyan ibn Husayn alone transmitted it from al-Hakam." The group of compilers transmitted it from Ibrahim al-Taymi. It is in the two Sahihs without the words "it sets in a hot spring," and its opening is: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ sitting," and so on.]]

He said: "It sets in a hot spring." This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, Ibn Umar, Ibn Amr and al-Hasan. Ibn Abbas recited ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (muddy). Ibn Abbas was with Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya recited ﴿حَامِيَةٍ﴾ (hot), and Ibn Abbas said: "Muddy (ḥamiʾa)." Mu'awiya said to Abd Allah ibn Amr: "How do you recite it?" He said: "As the Commander of the Faithful recites." Then he sent for Ka'b al-Ahbar: "How do you find the sun setting?" He said: "In water and mud. So we find it in the Torah." It is also reported: "In ṭīn (clay)." This agreed with Ibn Abbas's view. There was a man present who recited the verse of Tubba':

"He saw the sun's setting at its return,
in a spring of dark mud and black clay."

[[Dhu al-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim,
a king before whom kings submit and prostrate.
He reached the wests and the easts, seeking
the means of a command from a wise, rightly guided One.
He saw the place of the sun's setting at its return
in a spring of dark mud and black clay.

This is of Tubba' al-Akbar, the Yemeni mentioned in the Qur'an, who boasts of his grandfather Alexander Dhu al-Qarnayn, son of the Greek philosopher. It is also narrated with "mar" in place of "jaddi." "Tadin" means submits. It is narrated instead: "he rose high in the land, not disbelieving," meaning not denying, so there is no fault in the rhyme. "Khalab," with two vowels, is slime, which is mud. "Tha'at" is slime mixed with water, which increases moisture and spoils. "Ḥarmad" is black mud. He praised Dhu al-Qarnayn, then said he reached the places of the sun's setting and rising, seeking from God the means to reach his goal. He saw the place of the sun's setting at its return, that is, its coming back to him. It is also narrated: "the sun's setting at its disappearance," that is, its vanishing.

"Fi 'ayn" (in a spring) is connected to "ghār" (setting place), or to something omitted, meaning: he saw it setting in a spring. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "maghār," since the spring is wider than it, meaning: in a spring of water with black mud mixed with water. This agrees with the apparent meaning of the verse. Abu Ali al-Jubba'i interpreted it as being a matter of appearance (takhyil), as one who does not see the far shore of a vast sea sees the sun setting in it, when in reality it sets in darkness beyond the white, because the earth is spherical.]]

That is, in a spring of water with black mud and slime. There is no contradiction between ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (muddy) and ﴿حَامِيَةٍ﴾ (hot), for the spring may combine both qualities.

They were disbelievers, so God gave him the choice between punishing them by killing and calling them to Islam. He chose the call and striving to win them over. He said: "As for one who persists in wrongdoing, refusing anything but to remain upon the great wrong which is shirk (associating partners with God), that one is punished in both worlds." ﴿وَأَمَّا مَنْ آمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحاً فَلَهُ جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَى﴾ (But as for whoever believes and does righteousness, he shall have the best reward). It was said he gave them the choice between killing and captivity, and called the captivity a kindness in return for killing. ﴿فَلَهُ جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَى﴾ means he has the right to be rewarded with the best reward. Or it means: he has the reward of the good deed, which is the word of testimony. It is read: ﴿فَلَهُ جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَى﴾, meaning: the good deed is his reward.

It is related from Qatada: "He used to boil those who disbelieved in cauldrons, and that is the dreadful punishment. Whoever believed, he gave and clothed." ﴿مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْراً﴾ (of Our command, ease) means we do not command him with what is difficult and hard, but with what is easy and manageable, such as zakat, kharaj (land tax), and other things. Its implied sense is "one of ease," like the words ﴿قَوْلاً مَيْسُوراً﴾ (a gentle word). It is also read ﴿يُسْراً﴾ with two vowels.

It has been said that two believers ruled the earth, Dhu al-Qarnayn and Sulayman, and two disbelievers, Nimrod and Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it through Mujahid. It was also said that he was a prophet, and it was said that he was an angel.

It was said that he used to call them to monotheism (tawhid, affirming the oneness of God), and they would kill him, and God would bring him back to life.

And from him: the two sides of his head were of copper. It was also said that his crown had two horns, and that on his head was something resembling two horns.

It is possible that he was given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram (kabsh) because he butts his rivals. He was from the Romans, the son of an old woman who had no other child.

It was narrated by al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif, through Abd al-Aziz ibn Imran, from Sulayman ibn Asid, from al-Zuhri, who said: "He was only named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the horn of the sun at its setting and the horn of the sun at its rising."]], meaning its two sides, east and west. It was also said that he had two horns, that is, two braids. It was said that two generations of people passed away in his time. It is related from Wahb that he was called so because he ruled the Romans and the Persians, and it is also reported that he ruled the Romans and the Turks. And from him: the two sides of his head were of copper. It was also said that his crown had two horns, and that on his head was something resembling two horns.

It is possible that he was given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram (kabsh) because he butts his rivals. He was from the Romans, the son of an old woman who had no other child.

The questioners were the Jews, who asked him as a test. It was also said that Abu Jahl and his followers asked him. The address in ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (upon you) is to one of the two groups. ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ (from everything) means from the means of everything, namely the things he desired among his aims and purposes in his kingdom. ﴿سَبَباً﴾ (a means) means a path leading to it. A sabab (means) is that by which one reaches a goal, whether knowledge, power, or equipment. So he desired to reach the west, and ﴿فَأَتْبَعَ سَبَباً﴾ (then he followed a means) that would bring him there, until he arrived. Likewise he desired the east, and he followed a means, and he desired to reach the two barriers, and he followed a means.

It is read ﴿فَأَتْبَعَ﴾ (then he followed) with a different vowelling. It is read ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (muddy), from ḥamiʾat al-bi'r, when the well becomes filled with mud (ḥamʾa). And ﴿حَامِيَةٍ﴾ (hot) means "ḥārra" (burning).

It is related from Abu Dharr: "I was riding behind the Messenger of God ﷺ on a camel, and he saw the sun when it set, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where this sets?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It sets in a hot spring.'"

[[This is so in copies of al-Kashshaf: "on a camel." But in the books of hadith it is "on a donkey," and riding behind is not mentioned. It is related by Abu Dawud and al-Hakim through al-Hakam ibn Utayba, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, from his father, from Abu Dharr, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I was with the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he was on a donkey, and the sun was setting. He said: 'Do you know where this sets?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It sets in a hot spring.'" Al-Hakim added: "not hamzated" [i.e., ḥāmiya without hamza]. It was also narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, and added: "And it goes on until it prostrates before its Lord beneath the Throne. When it is time for it to rise, God permits it, and when God wants to make it rise from its west, He holds it back and says: 'Rise from where you set.' That is the time when faith will not benefit a soul." Al-Hakim said: "Sufyan ibn Husayn alone transmitted it from al-Hakam." The group of compilers transmitted it from Ibrahim al-Taymi. It is in the two Sahihs without the words "it sets in a hot spring," and its opening is: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ sitting," and so on.]]

He said: "It sets in a hot spring." This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, Ibn Umar, Ibn Amr and al-Hasan. Ibn Abbas recited ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (muddy). Ibn Abbas was with Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya recited ﴿حَامِيَةٍ﴾ (hot), and Ibn Abbas said: "Muddy (ḥamiʾa)." Mu'awiya said to Abd Allah ibn Amr: "How do you recite it?" He said: "As the Commander of the Faithful recites." Then he sent for Ka'b al-Ahbar: "How do you find the sun setting?" He said: "In water and mud. So we find it in the Torah." It is also reported: "In ṭīn (clay)." This agreed with Ibn Abbas's view. There was a man present who recited the verse of Tubba':

"He saw the sun's setting at its return,
in a spring of dark mud and black clay."

[[Dhu al-Qarnayn was my grandfather, a Muslim,
a king before whom kings submit and prostrate.
He reached the wests and the easts, seeking
the means of a command from a wise, rightly guided One.
He saw the place of the sun's setting at its return
in a spring of dark mud and black clay.

This is of Tubba' al-Akbar, the Yemeni mentioned in the Qur'an, who boasts of his grandfather Alexander Dhu al-Qarnayn, son of the Greek philosopher. It is also narrated with "mar" in place of "jaddi." "Tadin" means submits. It is narrated instead: "he rose high in the land, not disbelieving," meaning not denying, so there is no fault in the rhyme. "Khalab," with two vowels, is slime, which is mud. "Tha'at" is slime mixed with water, which increases moisture and spoils. "Ḥarmad" is black mud. He praised Dhu al-Qarnayn, then said he reached the places of the sun's setting and rising, seeking from God the means to reach his goal. He saw the place of the sun's setting at its return, that is, its coming back to him. It is also narrated: "the sun's setting at its disappearance," that is, its vanishing.

"Fi 'ayn" (in a spring) is connected to "ghār" (setting place), or to something omitted, meaning: he saw it setting in a spring. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "maghār," since the spring is wider than it, meaning: in a spring of water with black mud mixed with water. This agrees with the apparent meaning of the verse. Abu Ali al-Jubba'i interpreted it as being a matter of appearance (takhyil), as one who does not see the far shore of a vast sea sees the sun setting in it, when in reality it sets in darkness beyond the white, because the earth is spherical.]]

That is, in a spring of water with black mud and slime. There is no contradiction between ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (muddy) and ﴿حَامِيَةٍ﴾ (hot), for the spring may combine both qualities.

They were disbelievers, so God gave him the choice between punishing them by killing and calling them to Islam. He chose the call and striving to win them over. He said: "As for one who persists in wrongdoing, refusing anything but to remain upon the great wrong which is shirk (associating partners with God), that one is punished in both worlds." ﴿وَأَمَّا مَنْ آمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحاً فَلَهُ جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَى﴾ (But as for whoever believes and does righteousness, he shall have the best reward). It was said he gave them the choice between killing and captivity, and called the captivity a kindness in return for killing. ﴿فَلَهُ جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَى﴾ means he has the right to be rewarded with the best reward. Or it means: he has the reward of the good deed, which is the word of testimony. It is read: ﴿فَلَهُ جَزَاءً الْحُسْنَى﴾, meaning: the good deed is his reward.

It is related from Qatada: "He used to boil those who disbelieved in cauldrons, and that is the dreadful punishment. Whoever believed, he gave and clothed." ﴿مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْراً﴾ (of Our command, ease) means we do not command him with what is difficult and hard, but with what is easy and manageable, such as zakat, kharaj (land tax), and other things. Its implied sense is "one of ease," like the words ﴿قَوْلاً مَيْسُوراً﴾ (a gentle word). It is also read ﴿يُسْراً﴾ with two vowels.

Also read: maṭlaʿ, with a fatḥa on the lām, which is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The meaning is: he reached the place where the sun rises, as in the line of al-Nābigha:

Kaʾanna majarra al-rāmisāti dhuyūlahā [Kaʾanna majarra al-rāmisāti dhuyūlahā ... ʿalayhi qadīmun nammaqathu al-ṣawāniʿu]

Here majarr (the trailing) is not a place of trailing; it is a verbal noun meaning "the trailing." For if it were a noun of place, it would not govern the accusative. Moreover, a genitive construction (muḍāf) must be assumed for the predication "qaḍīm" to be valid, that is, "the place of trailing." So the sense is: the ground upon which the sweeping winds trail their skirts is a qaḍīm, meaning a white hide that craftsmen have embellished and beautified for writing. The winds are called rāmisāt from rams (ramas), meaning concealment, because they carry dust and cast it upon traces, burying them. He used "dhuyūl" (skirts) metaphorically for what the winds sweep over the earth, as an explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya). It is also permissible to liken the winds to women whose garments have long trains that they drag over the ground, in which case "dhuyūl" is an imaginative metaphor (takhyīl).

He means: as if the traces of the trailing of the sweeping winds were upon a people. It was said they were the Zanj. The sitr (screen/cover) is the buildings. It is related from Kaʿb:

"Their land does not hold buildings, and there are swarms in it. When the sun rises, they enter it, and when the day has risen high, they come out to their livelihoods."

It is also related from some men: "I went on until I passed China, and I asked about these people, and it was said: between you and them is a journey of a day and a night. So I reached them, and one of them would spread out one ear and wear the other. With me was a companion who knew their language, and they said to him: 'Have you come to see how the sun rises?' He said: 'While we were like that, we heard something like the sound of a clattering (ṣalṣala)'—[the note: in the Ṣiḥāḥ, ṣalla is the singular of ṣalāl, which are scattered drops of rain, one falling after another, and ṣalṣalat al-lijām is its sound when doubled. (ʿ)]—'and I fainted. Then I came to, and they were rubbing me with oil. When the sun rose over the water, it was above the water like the appearance of oil. They took us into a cave of theirs, and when the day rose high, they went out to the sea and began to catch fish and throw them in the sun, and it would cook for them.'"

It was also said: the sitr is clothing. It is related from Mujāhid: "Those of the Sudan who do not wear clothes at the rising of the sun are more numerous than all the people of the earth."

Thus (kadhālika): the matter of Dhū al-Qarnayn was thus, that is, as We have described it, to magnify his affair. "And We had encompassed what was with him" (wa-qad aḥaṭnā bi-mā ladayhi) with the armies, instruments, and means of kingship, "in full knowledge" (khubran), to increase the magnitude of that.

It was also said: "We did not make for them any shelter beside it, like that shelter We made for you from mountains, fortresses, buildings, shelters of every kind, and garments of every variety." And it was said: he reached the rising of the sun in the same way as he reached its setting. And it was said: he would come upon a people like that tribe upon whom he set in the west, meaning that they are unbelievers like them, and their judgment is like theirs: his punishing those among them who remained in disbelief, and his kindness toward those among them who believed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verses 92–93:

Between the two barriers (bayna al-saddayn): between the two mountains, and they are two mountains, the barrier of Dhu al-Qarnayn (the barrier built by Dhu al-Qarnayn) is between them. It is read with a ḍamma and with a fatḥa.

It was said: what is of the creation of Allah the Exalted is with a ḍamma, and what is of the work of the servants is with a fatḥa, because al-sadd with a ḍamma is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (fi'l bi-ma'na maf'ul), meaning: it is something that Allah the Exalted made and created. And al-sadd with a fatḥa is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of an action that people perform.

Bayna is in the accusative because it is an object (maf'ul bihi) that has been reached (mablugh), just as it is put in the genitive through annexation in His saying ﴿This is a parting between me and you﴾ [18:78], and as it is in the nominative in His saying ﴿Surely your bond has been severed﴾ [6:94], because it is one of the adverbial expressions (al-zuruf) that are used both as nouns and as adverbs. This place lies at the furthest end of the land of the Turks, on the side facing the east.

﴿Beyond them He found a people﴾: they are the Turks. ﴿Who scarcely understood any speech﴾: who could scarcely understand speech except with effort and hardship, through gestures and the like, as the mute are understood. It is also read as yafqahūna (yafqahūna), meaning: the listener does not understand their speech and they do not clarify it, because their language is strange and unknown.

It is also read as yafqahūna (yafqahūna), meaning: the listener does not understand their speech and they do not clarify it, because their language is strange and unknown.

Yājūj and Majūj are two foreign (ʿajamī) names, as shown by their being diptote (not taking tanwīn, with the ending "-ū" unnunated). They have also been read with hamza (Yāʾjūj/Māʾjūj). Ruʾba read them as Ājūj and Majūj. They are of the progeny of Yāfith. It has been said that Yājūj are from the Turks, and Majūj from the Jīl and the Daylam [[Al-Zamakhshari's phrase "min al-Jīl wa al-Daylam" is also how al-Nasafi gives it, and perhaps it is "min jīl al-Daylam." In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: jīl min al-nās, meaning a kind or class; the Turks are a jīl, and the Romans are a jīl. And in it: the Daylam are a jīl of people. (ʿ: the commentator al-ʿAqqāsh/annotator.)]] ... corrupters in the land. It has been said: they used to eat people. It was also said: they would emerge in the spring and leave nothing green without eating it, nor anything dry without carrying it off, and they would inflict on people great killing and harm. And it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ concerning their description: none of them dies until he sees a thousand male descendants of his own loins, all of whom have borne arms [[Recorded by Ibn ʿAdī, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Thaʿlabī and others, through the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq from al-Aʿmash, from Shaqīq, from Ḥudhayfah, who said: "I asked the Prophet ﷺ about Yājūj and Majūj, and he said: Yājūj is a nation, and Majūj is a nation. Each nation is four thousand; no man of them dies until he sees a thousand male descendants of his own loins, all of whom have borne arms." Ibn ʿAdī said: this is fabricated (mawḍūʿ). This Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq is not the author of the Maghāzī; rather he is al-ʿAkkāsh. Ibn al-Jawzī mentioned it among the fabricated reports through this route, but he was not correct, for it has another route: in Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān, from Ibn Masʿūd, traced to the Prophet: "Yājūj and Majūj: the least that one of them leaves for his loins is a thousand." In al-Nasāʾī, from ʿAmr ibn Aws, from his father, traced to the Prophet: "Yājūj and Majūj have intercourse as they wish, and no man of them dies without leaving behind from his offspring a thousand or more." In al-Mustadrak, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, traced to the Prophet: "Yājūj and Majūj are from the progeny of Ādam, and no man of them dies without leaving behind from his offspring a thousand or more."]]. It has also been said that they are of two kinds: tall ones, excessively tall, and short ones, excessively short. It is read: Kharajā and Kharājā, meaning they would make us pay from our wealth; its parallel is: al-nawl and al-nawāl. It is also read: Saddā and Sudda, with fatḥah and ḍammah.

﴿What my Lord has established me in is better﴾ — that is, what my Lord has granted me of abundant wealth and affluence is better than what you offer me in tribute (kharaj). So I have no need of it, just as Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: ﴿What God has given me is better than what He has given you﴾. It is read with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters) and with fakk (the letters kept separate). ﴿So help me with strength﴾: with workmen and craftsmen who are skilled in building and work, and with tools. ﴿A barrier﴾: a strong, fortified, well-bonded barrier. The radm is greater than the sadd, from their saying: "a garment mudamm," meaning patches upon patches.

It was said: they dug down to the foundation until they reached water, and made the foundation of rock and molten copper, and the structure of blocks of iron, with wood and charcoal between them until they filled the gap between the two mountains up to their summits. Then they placed the bellows, until it became like fire, and poured molten copper over the heated iron, so that it mixed and clung together and became a solid mountain.

It was also said: the distance between the two barriers was a hundred farsakhs.

It is also read as sawwa and sawwaa.

It is narrated from the Messenger of God ﷺ that a man informed him about it, and he said: "How did you see it?" He said: "Like the striped cloak (burd muhabbar), a black stripe and a red stripe." He said: "You have seen it."

[[Al-Tabari narrated it through the transmission of Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah from Qatadah. He said: "It was mentioned to us that a man said: 'O Messenger of God, I have seen the barrier of Yajuj and Majuj.' He said: 'Describe it to me.' He said: 'Like the striped cloak, a black stripe and a red stripe.' He said: 'You have seen it.'" Ibn Abi 'Umar narrated it from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah from Sa'id from Qatadah from a man of the people of Madinah, that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I have seen the barrier," and he mentioned something similar. Al-Tabarani narrated it in Musnad al-Shamiyyin. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from him through the transmission of Sa'id ibn Bashir from Qatadah from a man from Abu Bakrah al-Thaqafi: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ," and he mentioned something similar, but he said: "A red stripe of copper and a black stripe of iron." Al-Bazzar also narrated it from another route, from Yusuf ibn Abi Maryam al-Hanafi, who said: "While I was sitting with Abu Bakrah, a man came and greeted him. Abu Bakrah said to him: 'Who are you?' Everything that is spread out after being raised has been leveled (indakka). From this comes the phrase "al-jamal al-adak" (a camel with a flat hump), meaning one whose hump is flattened. It has also been read as "dakka'" with a long vowel (dakkā'), meaning a level ground. ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true﴾, the final part being a report of the words of Dhu al-Qarnayn.

And We left them, [making] some of them surge against others (ja'alna ba'dahum... ba'da al-khalq yamuju fi ba'd): that is, the creatures will surge and mingle, their humans and jinn bewildered (hayarā).

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj, meaning that they will surge when they come out from behind the barrier (al-sadd), crowding into the lands.

It is narrated that they will come to the sea, drink its water and eat its creatures, then eat the trees, and whoever of the people they overpower who has not fortified himself. They will not be able to reach Makkah, Madinah and Bayt al-Maqdis. Then Allah will send a worm (naghaf) into their necks, [[The author's note on "Allah will send a worm (naghaf) into their necks": that is, a worm, as stated in al-Sihah. (Ṣ)]] which enters their ears, and they die.

And We shall present Hell that day to the disbelievers, displayed before them, so that they see it and witness it. ﴿Those whose eyes were under a veil from My remembrance﴾: from My reminder, that is, from My signs which they would look upon and so be reminded to magnify Me. "My servants apart from Me as protectors" — these are the angels, meaning that they will not be protectors for them, as He related of them: "Glory be to You! You are our protector, not them" (Qur'an 34:41).

Ibn Mas'ud read: "Do those who disbelieve think..." (afaẓanna alladhīna kafarū). The reading of ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) is afa-ḥasiba alladhīna kafarū, meaning: "Is it sufficient for those who disbelieve..." — i.e., does it suffice them and do they reckon that they may take them as protectors? This is on the basis of the subject-predicate construction (al-ibtidāʾ wa'l-khabar), or on the basis of verb and agent (al-fiʿl wa'l-fāʿil), because when the active participle (ism al-fāʿil) depends on the interrogative hamza, it equals the verb in governing, as in your saying: aqāʾimun al-Zaydāni (are the two Zayds standing?). The meaning is that this does not suffice them nor benefit them with Allah, as they reckoned.

This is a sound and good reading. The nuzul (nuzl) is what is prepared for the guest (nazīl), i.e., the visitor, and similar to it is: "So give them good tidings of a painful punishment" (Qur'an 9:34; 84:24).

Their striving is lost, wasted, and they are the monks. This is from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, as in His words, *"Laboring and weary"* (88:3). From Mujahid: they are the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*). From Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him about them, and he said, "Among them are the people of Harura'."

From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "People will come on the Day of Resurrection with deeds that seem to them as large as the mountains of Tihama, but when they are weighed, they will not weigh anything." *"So We shall not set up for them any weight on the Day of Resurrection"* (18:105), meaning that We will not esteem them, and they will have no weight or value with Us.

It was also said: no scale will be set up for them, because the scale is only placed for the people of good and evil deeds among the monotheists (*al-muwahhidun*).

It was read *"fa-la yuqimu"* (with the verb in the third person, with a *ya'*). 

If you ask: in what position are *"alladhina dalla sa'yuhum"* (those whose striving is lost)? I say: the most probable is that they are in the nominative case, meaning "they are those whose striving is lost," because it is an answer to a question. It is also permissible that they be in the accusative, as a expression of blame, or in the genitive, as an apposition (*badal*). *Jahannam* is an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) to *"jaza'uhum"* (their recompense).

Al-Hawl: al-tahawwul (transformation, moving away). It is said: "He moved from his place (hala min makanihi) hawlan," just as you say: "Her love returned to me (adanee hubbuha) ʿawdan," meaning:

There is nothing beyond it, until their souls seek (tunāziʿuhum) what is most comprehensive of their aims and desires. This is the ultimate description, for a person in this world, in whatever bliss he may be, has his gaze raised toward something higher than it. It is also permissible that what is intended is the negation of transformation and the affirmation of eternity.

Al-Midad: the name for that with which the inkwell is replenished with ink, and that with which the lamp is replenished with oil (al-saliṭ). It is said: "The sky is the midad of the earth." The meaning: "If the words of God's knowledge and wisdom were written, and the sea were ink for them, [the sea would be exhausted] — and by the sea is meant the genus — the sea would be exhausted before the words were exhausted. And even if We brought the like of it as ink, it would also be exhausted."

"And the words are not exhausted." Madadan is a tamyiz (specification), like your saying: "I have the like of it, a man." Al-madad is like al-midad, and it is that with which something is replenished. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "bi-mithlihi midadan." Al-Aʿraj read: "maddan," with a kasra on the mim, plural of muddah, which is what the scribe draws upon so that he writes with it. It has also been read: "yanfada" with a ya'. It is said: Ḥuyayy ibn Akhtab said: "In your scripture: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾, then you recite: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾." So it was revealed, meaning: that is a great good, but it is a drop from the sea of the words of Allah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 18, verse 110:

﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾: whoever hopes for a good meeting with his Lord, and that he meets Him in a state of good pleasure and acceptance.

We have already explained "the meeting" (al-liqa'). Or it is read: "Is one who fears the evil of his meeting [with Him]...?"

The prohibition of associating anyone in worship is meant as: that one should not show off in his deed, and should seek by it nothing but the Face of his Lord, sincerely, without mixing anything else with it. It was said: it was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Zuhayr, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I perform a deed for God, but when someone looks at it, it pleases me." So he (ﷺ) said:

"God does not accept what is associated with Him in it [[Al-Wahidi transmitted it in al-Asbab from Ibn 'Abbas, without giving its chain of narration.]]." It is also narrated that he said: "For you are two rewards: the reward of the secret, and the reward of the open." [[Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated it, and Ibn Hibban, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, from Abu Hurayrah. A man said: "O Messenger of God, I perform a deed and someone sees it, and it pleases me." He said: "For you are two rewards: the reward of the secret, and the reward of the open." They all narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Sinan, Sa'id ibn Sinan, from Harb ibn Abi Thabit, from Abu Salih, from him. Al-Tirmidhi said: al-A'mash narrated it from Habib, from Abu Salih, as a mursal (broken chain). Ibn Abi Hatim said: my father said, "The correct one in my view is mursal; Yusuf ibn Asbat narrated it from al-Thawri, from Habib."

From Abu Salih, from Abu Dharr. Abu Nu'aym also narrated it in al-Hilyah and said: no one has said "from Abu Dharr" except Ibn Asbat. Yahya ibn al-Yaman narrated it from al-Thawri and said "from Ibn Mas'ud." Al-Tabarani narrated it, Abu Nu'aym said. Qabisah narrated it from al-Thawri and said "from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, may God be pleased with him."] And that is when one intends to be followed as an example. And from him (ﷺ): "Beware of the minor shirk." They said: "What is the minor shirk?" He said: "Showing off (al-riya')." [[Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from al-'Ala', from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, in this wording, and by this route al-Tha'labi narrated it, and Abu Qasim al-Talhi in al-Targhib. There is also a report on this subject from Mahmud ibn Labid, which he raised: "What I fear most for you is the minor shirk." They said, "O Messenger of God, what is the minor shirk?" He said, "Showing off." Ahmad and al-Daraqutni (in Gharib Malik) and al-Bayhaqi (in al-Shu'ab) narrated it from the narration of 'Amr ibn Abi 'Amr, from Qatadah, from him. And from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: "In the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) we counted showing off as the minor shirk." Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it. In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.]] And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever reads Surat al-Kahf from its end, there will be a light for him from his forehead to his feet, and whoever reads it all, there will be a light for him from the earth to the sky. [[Ahmad and al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Anas. In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah. Al-Tabarani narrated it from the narration of Rushdin ibn Sa'd; both of them from Ziyad ibn Fayd, and they are among the weak narrators.]]" And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever reads at his bed, 'Say: I am only a human like you,' there will be for him from his bed a light shining to Makkah, filled with that light by angels who send blessings upon him until he rises. And if his bed is in Makkah, there will be for him a light shining from his bed to the House al-Ma'mur, filled with that light by angels who send blessings upon him until he awakes." [[Ishaq and al-Bazzar narrated it from the narration of al-Nadr ibn Shumayl: Abu Farwah al-Asadi, a man from the people of the desert, told us: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrate from 'Umar, raised: "Whoever reads in his night, 'Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord...' the verse, there will be for him a light from 'Adn to Makkah, filled by the angels." Al-Tha'labi narrated it by this route, adding: "they send blessings upon him and ask forgiveness for him." Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b with the first wording, and its chain has already passed in Al 'Imran.]] And God knows best.
